docs.title: About this book
docs.text: A complete first course in German for English speakers, from the sounds and letters of the language to telling a friend what you did at the weekend. Each of the sixteen lessons opens with a short dialogue, gives the vocabulary in a table, explains one or two points of grammar step by step, and ends with a cultural note on Germany, Austria and Switzerland, a summary, exercises with answers and a quiz. Every German word and sentence can be heard aloud, and every noun is shown in the colour of its gender. The course covers the A1 level of the Common European Framework and the first steps of A2.

docs.title: About this book
docs.text:
Herzlich willkommen!

This is a first course in German for English speakers. It starts from nothing, not even the alphabet, and takes you in sixteen lessons to the point where you can introduce yourself, talk about your family, your home and your day, order a meal, buy food at a market, ask the way, make plans with friends and tell someone what you did at the weekend. In the terms of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages, it covers level A1 completely and the first part of A2.

German is the language with the largest number of native speakers in the European Union. It is the official language of Germany and Austria, one of the official languages of Switzerland, Belgium and Luxembourg, and the official language of Liechtenstein. For an English speaker it is a close relative: English and German both descend from the West Germanic branch of the Indo-European family, and you will recognise hundreds of everyday words at once, such as Haus, Hand, Finger, Wasser, Butter, Buch and Mann. German grammar has more endings than English, but they follow clear patterns, and its spelling is far more regular: once you know the rules of Lesson 1, you can pronounce almost any German word you see.

docs.title: Who this book is for
docs.text:
The book is written for adult and teenage learners whose first or strongest language is English and who have studied little or no German. You may be learning for travel, for work or study in a German-speaking country, for a first university course, to talk with family or friends, or simply for pleasure. No knowledge of grammar is assumed: every term is explained when it first appears, and the Glossary at the end collects them all. If you learnt some German at school long ago, the first lessons will come back quickly, and the later ones will give you the structures that make the language fit together.

You can work through the book alone, with a teacher, or with a partner. Everything you need is on the page: dialogues you can hear, explanations, practice, and answers.

docs.title: How the book is organised
docs.text:
The sixteen lessons are grouped in four parts.

Part Lessons What you learn I · First steps 1 to 4 Sounds and spelling, umlauts, ß and ch; greetings and introductions; numbers, dates and time; nouns, their gender and their plurals II · The present 5 to 8 Articles, sein and haben; the present tense; word order and questions; the accusative III · Everyday life 9 to 12 Family and describing people; food and shopping; the city, directions and the dative; modal verbs IV · Plans and memories 13 to 16 Daily routine and separable verbs; the perfect tense; travel, weather and plans; a final review

Table 1. The plan of the course.

At the end of the book are the Verb Tables, with every verb pattern of the course; a Glossary of grammar terms and troublesome words; and a short list of Further Reading.

docs.title: How to use a lesson
docs.text:
Every lesson has the same nine parts, so you always know where you are.

  1. Learning outcomes. What you will be able to do at the end. Read them first, and come back to them at the end.
  2. Dialogue. A short scene in German, with an English translation, that uses the language of the lesson. Listen to it, read it, and read it aloud. The same characters appear throughout: Emma, a young Englishwoman who has come to Leipzig for a German course; Jonas, a German student who shares a flat with her; their teacher, Frau Wagner; Emma's classmate Ravi, from India; and Jonas's cousin Sophie, who lives in Vienna.
  3. Vocabulary. The new words and phrases, in tables, with a sound guide for the harder ones.
  4. Grammar. Usually two sections, each explaining one point step by step, from the idea to the forms, with examples and a worked example.
  5. Practice. Tables to fill in from memory, sentences to say aloud, and a speaking task.
  6. Culture. A note on life and language in Germany, Austria and Switzerland.
  7. Summary. The essentials of the lesson in a few lines. Reread it before you start the next lesson.
  8. Exercises. Questions with answers folded underneath. Try each one before you open the answer.
  9. Quiz. A set of questions of different kinds to check what you have learnt.

Aim to spend several sessions on each lesson rather than one long one. Short, regular practice works far better than long, occasional sessions: twenty minutes a day will take you further than three hours on a Sunday. Say everything aloud, even when you are alone. Go back to earlier lessons often; each review makes the language more automatic.

Learn phrases, not only words

Learn whole phrases such as Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee, bitte. or Wie komme ich zum Bahnhof? as they are, before you understand every part of them. The grammar sections explain the parts later, and by then you will already be using them.

docs.title: Colours, sounds and practice
docs.text:
This book is meant to be heard as well as read. Every German word, phrase and sentence has a listen button beside it: press it to hear the phrase, and press again to hear it slowly. A dialogue or a list of phrases also has a Play all button that reads it from start to finish.

Gender colours. Every German noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, and the gender decides the form of the words around it (Lesson 4). To help you remember, the book shows each noun in the colour of its gender wherever it is listed with its article:

masculine: derfeminine: dieneuter: dasplural: die

Masculine nouns are blue, feminine nouns pink, plurals violet, and neuter nouns are left in the plain colour of the text: der Tisch, die Lampe, das Buch, die Bücher. The article is always printed with the noun, so the gender is never shown by colour alone.

  • Sound guides. New words have an approximate pronunciation in square brackets, using English spelling, with the stressed syllable in capitals: danke [DAHN-kuh]. Lesson 1 explains how to read them, including the three sounds that English does not have. They help, but the recordings are the real model.
  • Practice tables. A table with a Practice switch hides its key forms and turns them into boxes for you to fill in; Check marks your answers.
  • Typed answers. Many exercises have a box in which to type your answer and check it before you open the model answer. If your keyboard has no umlauts, type the letter without its dots: the answer is accepted with a reminder of the correct spelling.
  • Quizzes. Each lesson ends with a quiz: multiple choice, gaps to fill, matching, words to put in order, a wrong word to find, sentences to listen to and write down, and phrases to say aloud. Your answers and best score are kept in your browser, so you can come back to a quiz later.
  • Speaking tasks. Boxes titled "Say it" ask you to speak. Where your browser can recognise speech, a microphone button lets you check your pronunciation.

docs.title: Which German?
docs.text:
German, like English, is one language with many accents and regional words. The book teaches standard German (Hochdeutsch), the form used in education, the media and writing in all German-speaking countries and understood everywhere. The culture notes and the vocabulary tables point out the main differences as they come up: the Austrian Grüß Gott and Servus, the Swiss Grüezi, the Austrian Jänner for January, the many words for a bread roll, and the Swiss habit of writing ss where Germany and Austria write ß.

You will also hear, especially in Switzerland and in the south, local dialects that differ a great deal from the standard language. Speakers of these dialects all learn standard German at school and will switch to it for you. Whichever accent you meet, the German of this book will be understood.

Also, los geht's! So, let's go!

docs.title: Lesson 5: Articles, the Nominative, sein and haben
docs.text:
Artikel, Nominativ, sein und haben

With nouns and their genders in place, you can now build real sentences about people and things. This lesson brings together four essentials. The first is the word for "a", which, like the word for "the", has a form for each gender: ein, eine, ein. The second is kein, "no, not a", German's way of saying that something is not there. The third is the idea of case, which explains why these words sometimes change; you meet the first case, the nominative, here. And the fourth is the pair of verbs you will use in almost every conversation: sein ("to be") and haben ("to have").

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • use the indefinite article ein, eine, ein and the negative article kein, keine, kein, keine;
  • use the possessives mein, dein and Ihr with nouns of every gender;
  • recognise the subject of a sentence and use the nominative case;
  • conjugate sein and haben, and use them where German and English differ (Ich habe Hunger, Ich bin zwanzig);
  • say what your job is, without an article: Ich bin Lehrerin;
  • choose between nicht and kein.

masculinefeminineneuterplural

docs.title: 5.1 Dialogue: the birthday party
docs.text:
Emma and Ravi arrive at Jonas's birthday party.

  • Jonas: Emma, Ravi, hallo! Kommt rein! — Emma, Ravi, hi! Come in!
  • Emma: Alles Gute zum Geburtstag, Jonas! Hier, ein Geschenk für dich. — Happy birthday, Jonas! Here, a present for you.
  • Jonas: Oh, danke! Das ist ein Buch! Super. — Oh, thanks! It's a book! Great.
  • Ravi: Wer ist die Frau da? Ist das deine Freundin? — Who is the woman there? Is that your girlfriend?
  • Jonas: Nein, das ist keine Freundin, das ist meine Schwester Lena. Sie ist Ärztin. — No, that's not a girlfriend, that's my sister Lena. She's a doctor.
  • Ravi: Und der Mann? Ist er auch Arzt? — And the man? Is he a doctor too?
  • Jonas: Nein, das ist mein Bruder Tim. Er ist Koch. Habt ihr Hunger? — No, that's my brother Tim. He's a cook. Are you hungry?
  • Ravi: Ja, ich habe Hunger! Und Durst. — Yes, I'm hungry! And thirsty.
  • Jonas: Die Pizza ist in der Küche, und die Getränke auch. — The pizza is in the kitchen, and the drinks too.
  • Lena: Hallo! Ich bin Lena. Bist du Emma aus England? — Hi! I'm Lena. Are you Emma from England?
  • Emma: Ja, genau. Und du bist Ärztin, oder? — Yes, exactly. And you're a doctor, aren't you?
  • Lena: Ja. Und was bist du von Beruf? — Yes. And what do you do for a living?
  • Emma: Ich bin Lehrerin, aber jetzt bin ich Studentin. Ich habe ein Jahr frei. — I'm a teacher, but now I'm a student. I have a year off.
  • Lena: Toll! Dein Deutsch ist sehr gut. — Great! Your German is very good.
  • Emma: Danke, du bist sehr nett. Aber ich habe noch viele Probleme mit der Grammatik! — Thanks, you're very kind. But I still have lots of problems with grammar!

Notice:

  1. "a" is ein or eine: ein Buch, ein Geschenk, ein Jahr. "Not a" is kein or keine: keine Freundin.
  2. "My" and "your" also change with the gender: mein Bruder, meine Schwester, deine Freundin, dein Deutsch.
  3. Jobs have no article: Sie ist Ärztin. Er ist Koch. ("She is a doctor. He is a cook.")
  4. German says "I have hunger": Ich habe Hunger.

docs.title: 5.3 Grammar: articles and the nominative case
What a case is
docs.text:
In English, he and him are the same person in different roles: He sees the dog but The dog sees him. These roles are called cases. English shows them only in a few pronouns (I / me, he / him, she / her, we / us, they / them, who / whom). German shows them also in the articles and possessives before nouns. German has four cases:

Case Main job Taught in nominative the subject: who or what does or is something this lesson accusative the direct object: who or what is affected Lesson 8 dative the indirect object, and after many prepositions Lesson 11 genitive possession ("of"), mostly in writing for recognition only

Table 5.5. The four cases.

The nominative is the case of the subject, the person or thing that does the action or that the sentence is about. It is also the case after sein ("to be") and heißen: in Das ist ein Buch, both das and ein Buch are in the nominative. All the forms you have learnt so far are nominative forms, and the nominative is the form in which nouns are listed in dictionaries.

To find the subject, ask who? (wer?) or what? (was?) before the verb: Mein Bruder ist Koch. Who is a cook? Mein Bruder: the subject, nominative.

docs.title: The indefinite article: ein, eine, ein
docs.text:
The word for "a" or "an" has a form for each gender. Masculine and neuter look the same; feminine adds -e. There is no plural, as in English: "a book", but "books".

Masculine Feminine Neuter Plural definite: the der Tisch die Lampe das Buch die Bücher indefinite: a ein Tisch eine Lampe ein Buch Bücher negative: no, not a kein Tisch keine Lampe kein Buch keine Bücher possessive: my mein Tisch meine Lampe mein Buch meine Bücher

Table 5.6. The articles and possessives in the nominative. Switch on Practice and fill them in.

The rule to remember: ein, kein and the possessives add -e for feminine and plural, and nothing for masculine and neuter. Learn one line and you have them all.

docs.title: The negative article kein
docs.text:
kein means "no", "not a" or "not any". It is the negative of ein and of nouns with no article, and it takes the same endings as ein, with a plural form keine:

  • Das ist ein Problem. → Das ist kein Problem. — That's no problem.
  • Das ist eine Freundin. → Das ist keine Freundin. — That's not a girlfriend.
  • Ich habe Zeit. → Ich habe keine Zeit. — I have no time.
  • Hier sind Stühle. → Hier sind keine Stühle. — There are no chairs here.

docs.title: The possessives mein, dein, Ihr
docs.text:
"My", "your" (familiar) and "your" (polite) are mein, dein and Ihr, and they take the same endings as ein:

  • mein Bruder, meine Schwester, mein Kind, meine Eltern
  • dein Name, deine Adresse, dein Handy, deine Freunde
  • Ihr Name, Ihre Adresse, Ihr Handy, Ihre Freunde

The ending depends on the noun that follows, not on the owner: Emma's brother is mein Bruder when she speaks, and Jonas's sister is meine Schwester when he speaks. Lesson 9 gives the possessives for every person (his, her, our, their).

docs.title: Jobs and nationalities without an article
docs.text:
After sein and werden ("to become"), German uses no article before a job, a nationality or a religion:

  • Ich bin Lehrerin. — I'm a teacher.
  • Er ist Koch. — He's a cook.
  • Sie ist Engländerin. — She's English (an Englishwoman).

To ask about someone's job, say Was sind Sie von Beruf? or Was bist du von Beruf? ("What are you by profession?"), or simply Was machst du beruflich?. The article comes back when you add an adjective: Er ist ein guter Koch. ("He's a good cook.")

Common mistake: Ich bin ein Lehrer

Ich bin ein Lehrer is a direct translation of I am a teacher, and it sounds wrong in German. Leave out the article: Ich bin Lehrer. And use the feminine form for a woman: Ich bin Lehrerin.

docs.title: The forms
docs.text:
sein and haben are irregular, as to be and to have are in English. They are the two most common verbs in the language, and you will also need them to form the past tense in Lesson 14. Learn them by heart.

Person sein (to be) haben (to have) ich bin habe du bist hast er, sie, es ist hat wir sind haben ihr seid habt sie, Sie sind haben

Table 5.7. The present of sein and haben.

Notice that ihr seid ("you are", plural) is spelt with a d, and that seit with a t is a different word ("since"). In haben, only the du and er forms are irregular: the b disappears, du hast, er hat.

docs.title: Sie, sie and sie
docs.text:
You can now see the three meanings of sie from Lesson 2 at work. The verb tells "she" apart from the other two; only the capital letter tells "they" from "you".

Figure 5.1 Three meanings of sie. A diagram with three columns. The first, "sie = she", shows the example "sie ist, sie hat, sie kommt", with the verb ending -t. The second, "sie = they", shows "sie sind, sie haben, sie kommen", with the verb ending -en. The third, "Sie = you (polite)", shows "Sie sind, Sie haben, Sie kommen", with the same -en and a capital S. A note below: at the start of a sentence, only the context tells they from polite you.

At the start of a sentence, where every word has a capital, only the context tells "they" from polite "you": Sie sind sehr nett. can mean "They are very nice" or "You are very nice".

docs.title: Using sein
docs.text:
sein links the subject to a description, a job, a place, an age or a name:

  • Ich bin müde. — I'm tired.
  • Lena ist Ärztin. — Lena is a doctor.
  • Wir sind in Leipzig. — We are in Leipzig.
  • Das ist mein Bruder. — This is my brother.
  • Jonas ist dreiundzwanzig. — Jonas is twenty-three.

The word after sein that describes the subject is in the nominative, like the subject itself: Der Mann ist mein Bruder.

docs.title: Using haben
docs.text:
haben means "to have", for what you own, your family, your time, and in many fixed phrases:

  • Ich habe ein Auto. — I have a car.
  • Hast du eine Schwester? — Have you got a sister?
  • Wir haben zwei Kinder. — We have two children.
  • Habt ihr heute Zeit? — Are you free today?

The thing you have is not the subject but the object of the sentence, and it is in a different case, the accusative. With feminine, neuter and plural nouns the accusative looks exactly like the nominative, so all the examples above are already correct. Only a masculine noun changes: ein becomes einen, kein becomes keinen, mein becomes meinen:

  • Ich habe einen Bruder. — I have a brother.
  • Er hat keinen Computer. — He has no computer.

Use these phrases as they are for now; Lesson 8 explains the accusative fully.

docs.title: Where German and English differ
docs.text:
Three everyday situations take haben or another construction in German where English uses "to be", or the other way round:

English German Not I'm hungry, I'm thirsty Ich habe Hunger. Ich habe Durst. Ich bin hungrig (possible, but much less common) I'm twenty Ich bin zwanzig. Ich habe zwanzig Jahre (as in French or Spanish) I'm cold, I'm hot Mir ist kalt. Mir ist warm. Ich bin kalt (this means "I am a cold person") I'm lucky Ich habe Glück. Ich bin glücklich (this means "I'm happy") You're right Du hast recht. Du bist richtig

Table 5.8. Differences between German and English. Learn Mir ist kalt as a fixed phrase: mir is "to me" (Lesson 11).

docs.title: Nicht or kein?
docs.text:
German has two words for "not". Choose by looking at what you are negating:

  • Use kein before a noun that would otherwise have ein or no article: Ich habe kein Auto. Das ist keine gute Idee. Wir haben keine Zeit.
  • Use nicht for everything else: with verbs, adjectives, names, and nouns with der, die, das or a possessive: Ich bin nicht müde. Das ist nicht mein Buch. Er ist nicht Jonas. Ich verstehe das nicht.

Worked example: negating sentences

Make each sentence negative.

  1. Das ist ein Problem. The noun has ein → kein: Das ist kein Problem.
  2. Ich habe Geschwister. ("brothers and sisters", plural, no article) → keine: Ich habe keine Geschwister.
  3. Das ist meine Tasche. The noun has a possessive → nicht: Das ist nicht meine Tasche.
  4. Lena ist verheiratet. An adjective → nicht: Lena ist nicht verheiratet.
  5. Ich habe einen Bruder. Masculine, accusative einen → keinen: Ich habe keinen Bruder.

docs.title: Who is it?
docs.text:
Read the description aloud, then describe two people you know in the same way.

  • Das ist meine Freundin Sophie. — This is my friend Sophie.
  • Sie ist sechsundzwanzig und wohnt in Wien. — She's twenty-six and lives in Vienna.
  • Sie ist Ingenieurin. — She's an engineer.
  • Sie hat einen Bruder, aber keine Schwester. — She has a brother, but no sister.
  • Sie ist nicht verheiratet. — She's not married.

Say it

Introduce yourself with sein and haben: your name, age, job, family, and how you feel today. For example:

Ich bin Ravi. Ich bin zweiunddreißig Jahre alt. Ich bin Informatiker. Ich habe eine Schwester. Heute bin ich müde, und ich habe Hunger.

docs.title: 5.6 Culture: work and job titles
docs.text:
What do you do? Germans tend to introduce themselves with their job more readily than with their hobbies, and a training is valued as much as a degree. Many young people in Germany, Austria and Switzerland learn a trade or profession through a dual vocational training (die duale Ausbildung): for two to three and a half years they work in a company and attend a vocational school at the same time. Cooks, mechanics, bank clerks, nurses, electricians and hundreds of other professions are trained this way, and the system is widely admired. A person in training is an Azubi, short for Auszubildende or Auszubildender.

Job titles for women and men. Almost every job title has a feminine form in -in, and it is normal to use it: a woman says Ich bin Ingenieurin, not Ingenieur. Job advertisements must be open to all and usually show this in the title, for example Verkäufer (m/w/d), for männlich, weiblich, divers (male, female, diverse).

Talking about groups. When speaking of a mixed group, German traditionally used the masculine plural: die Lehrer for all teachers. Today many speakers, institutions and newspapers prefer forms that name both, and you will meet several of them: Lehrerinnen und Lehrer; neutral words such as die Lehrkräfte (teaching staff) or die Studierenden (those who study); and written forms with a sign in the middle, such as Lehrer*innen or Lehrer:innen. These forms are the subject of lively public debate, and usage differs between people and organisations. As a learner, you should recognise them; in your own German, Lehrerinnen und Lehrer is always correct and polite.

docs.title: 5.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Cases: nominative (subject), accusative, dative, genitive. The nominative is used for the subject and after sein and heißen.
  • Indefinite article: ein (m), eine (f), ein (n); no plural.
  • Negative article: kein, keine, kein; plural keine. Possessives mein, dein, Ihr take the same endings.
  • sein: bin, bist, ist, sind, seid, sind. haben: habe, hast, hat, haben, habt, haben.
  • Jobs without article: Ich bin Lehrerin. Was sind Sie von Beruf?
  • German vs English: Ich habe Hunger / Durst. Ich bin zwanzig. Mir ist kalt. Du hast recht.
  • haben + masculine object: einen, keinen, meinen (Lesson 8).
  • kein for nouns with ein or no article; nicht for the rest.

docs.title: 5.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Complete with the right form of sein: Ihr ___ sehr nett.

Answer

seid. Ihr seid sehr nett. Spelt with d.

Exercise 2

Complete with the right form of haben: ___ du Durst?

Answer

Hast. Hast du Durst?

Exercise 3

Complete with ein or eine: Das ist ___ Wohnung.

Answer

eine. eine Wohnung. Wohnung is feminine.

Exercise 4

Complete with mein or meine: Das ist ___ Handy.

Answer

mein. mein Handy. Handy is neuter: no ending.

Exercise 5

Make negative with kein: Ich habe Zeit.

Answer

Ich habe keine Zeit. Ich habe keine Zeit. Zeit is feminine, so keine.

Exercise 6

Make negative: Das ist mein Kuli.

Answer

Das ist nicht mein Kuli. Das ist nicht mein Kuli. A noun with a possessive is negated with nicht.

Exercise 7

Translate: "She is a nurse."

Answer

Sie ist Krankenpflegerin. Sie ist Krankenpflegerin. No article, and the feminine form.

Exercise 8

Translate: "I'm hungry, but I'm not tired."

Answer

Ich habe Hunger, aber ich bin nicht müde.

Exercise 9

Correct the mistakes: Ich habe dreißig Jahre. Ich bin ein Arzt. Ich bin kalt.

Answer

Ich bin dreißig Jahre alt. Ich bin Arzt. Mir ist kalt. Age with sein; no article before a job; feeling cold is Mir ist kalt.

Exercise 10

Write four sentences about Tim: he is Jonas's brother, he is a cook, he has a car but no flat, and today he is happy.

Answer

Tim ist der Bruder von Jonas. Er ist Koch. Er hat ein Auto, aber keine Wohnung. Heute ist er glücklich.

docs.text:
Quiz: articles, sein and haben

Exercise 11

Wir ___ aus Indien.

  1. bin
  2. ist
  3. sind
  4. seid
Answer

docs.title: Lesson 13: Daily Routine and Separable Verbs
docs.text:
Der Alltag und die trennbaren Verben

Getting up, having a shower, getting dressed, setting off, shopping, tidying up, watching television, going out, falling asleep: the verbs of daily life are among the most useful in any language. In German, many of them belong to a special group, the separable verbs, whose first part breaks off and goes to the end of the sentence: aufstehen ("to get up") but Ich stehe um sieben auf. Many others are reflexive: they need a pronoun like myself, where English needs none: Ich ziehe mich an, "I get (myself) dressed". In this lesson you learn both groups, and the words that put the events of a day in order.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • describe your daily routine from morning to night;
  • use separable verbs such as aufstehen, anfangen, einkaufen, fernsehen in statements, questions, imperatives and with modal verbs;
  • recognise inseparable prefixes such as be-, er-, ver- and stress verbs correctly;
  • use reflexive verbs such as sich duschen, sich anziehen, sich beeilen with the reflexive pronouns;
  • put events in order with zuerst, dann, danach, später, zum Schluss;
  • say how often you do things with normalerweise, meistens, immer, oft, selten, nie.

docs.title: 13.1 Dialogue: an early morning
docs.text:
It is seven o'clock on a Monday. Jonas comes into the kitchen, half asleep. Emma is already having breakfast.

  • Jonas: Guten Morgen … Warum bist du schon so früh wach? — Good morning … Why are you awake so early?
  • Emma: Ich stehe jeden Tag um halb sieben auf. Mein Kurs fängt um acht an. — I get up at half past six every day. My course starts at eight.
  • Jonas: Halb sieben! Normalerweise stehe ich erst um neun auf. Aber heute muss ich früh zur Uni. — Half past six! I don't normally get up until nine. But today I have to go to university early.
  • Emma: Was machst du denn morgens? — So what do you do in the mornings?
  • Jonas: Zuerst dusche ich, dann ziehe ich mich an, und dann trinke ich einen Kaffee. Frühstück esse ich selten. — First I have a shower, then I get dressed, and then I drink a coffee. I rarely eat breakfast.
  • Emma: Ich frühstücke immer. Danach lese ich die Nachrichten, und um halb acht gehe ich los. — I always have breakfast. After that I read the news, and at half past seven I set off.
  • Jonas: Und wann kommst du nach Hause? — And when do you get home?
  • Emma: Um eins. Nachmittags kaufe ich ein oder räume auf, und abends sehe ich manchmal fern. — At one. In the afternoon I go shopping or tidy up, and in the evening I sometimes watch television.
  • Jonas: Heute Abend kommen Tim und Lena vorbei. Wir gehen zusammen aus. Kommst du mit? — Tim and Lena are coming round this evening. We're going out together. Are you coming?
  • Emma: Gern! Aber ich kann nicht lange bleiben. Morgen muss ich wieder früh aufstehen. — I'd love to! But I can't stay long. Tomorrow I have to get up early again.
  • Jonas: Kein Problem. Oh, schon zehn nach sieben! Ich muss mich beeilen. — No problem. Oh, ten past seven already! I have to hurry.
  • Emma: Dann beeil dich! Und vergiss deinen Schlüssel nicht! — Then hurry up! And don't forget your key!

Notice:

  1. aufstehen splits in two: Ich stehe um halb sieben auf. So do anfangen (fängt … an), einkaufen, aufräumen, fernsehen, vorbeikommen, ausgehen, mitkommen, losgehen.
  2. After a modal verb, the separable verb stays in one piece at the end: Morgen muss ich wieder früh aufstehen.
  3. Some verbs need a pronoun that refers back to the subject: ich ziehe mich an, ich muss mich beeilen, beeil dich!
  4. erst um neun means "not until nine".

docs.text:

docs.title: What a separable verb is
docs.text:
Many German verbs are made of a short prefix and a basic verb: auf + stehen, an + rufen, ein + kaufen, fern + sehen. Most of these prefixes are also prepositions or adverbs, and they change the meaning of the verb, rather like English get up, call up, come back, go out. In English the little word follows the verb; in German it is written in front of it in the infinitive, but separates from it in many sentences.

The common separable prefixes are: ab-, an-, auf-, aus-, ein-, fern-, los-, mit-, vor-, vorbei-, weg-, zu-, zurück-.

docs.title: Where the prefix goes
docs.text:
In the present (and the simple past), when the verb stands in position 2 or position 1, the prefix goes to the end of the sentence, forming a sentence bracket like the one in Lesson 12:

  • statement: Ich stehe jeden Tag um halb sieben auf.
  • W-question: Wann fängt der Kurs an?
  • yes-no question: Kommst du heute Abend mit?
  • imperative: Ruf mich morgen an! Räumt bitte euer Zimmer auf!

The verb part is conjugated as usual, including vowel changes: anfangen → er fängt an, fernsehen → du siehst fern, einladen → sie lädt ein, abfahren → der Zug fährt ab.

Figure 13.1 A separable verb. A diagram of a separable verb. At the top, the infinitive "aufstehen" is shown as two coloured blocks, "auf" in blue and "stehen" in orange. Arrows lead to the sentence "Ich – stehe – um sieben Uhr – auf.", with "stehe" in position 2 and "auf" at the end, joined by a bracket. Below, a second sentence with a modal verb: "Ich – muss – um sieben Uhr – aufstehen.", where the infinitive stays in one piece at the end. A note says that the prefix carries the stress: AUFstehen. Infinitive Sentence aufstehen Ich stehe um sieben auf. anfangen Der Film fängt um acht an. einkaufen Wir kaufen samstags ein. fernsehen Siehst du oft fern? anrufen Ruf mich bitte an! mitkommen Wer kommt heute mit?

Table 13.4. Practice: the verb in position 2 (or 1), the prefix at the end.

docs.title: When the verb does not separate
docs.text:
The prefix and the verb stay together, in one word, when the verb is in the infinitive at the end of the sentence, for example after a modal verb:

  • Morgen muss ich früh aufstehen.
  • Kannst du mich abholen?
  • Willst du mitkommen?

They also stay together in subordinate clauses (Lesson 16), and in the perfect tense the ge- of the past participle goes between them: aufgestanden, eingekauft (Lesson 14).

Common mistake: forgetting the prefix

The prefix is part of the meaning, so leaving it out changes the verb. Ich stehe um sieben means "I am standing at seven", which makes little sense; Ich stehe um sieben auf means "I get up at seven". Ich rufe meine Mutter means "I call out for my mother"; Ich rufe meine Mutter an means "I phone my mother". In a long sentence, listen right to the end: the prefix may be the last word.

docs.title: Inseparable prefixes
docs.text:
Eight prefixes never separate: be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss-, ver-, zer-. Verbs with them behave like ordinary verbs, and the prefix is not stressed:

  • besuchen: Ich besuche meine Oma. (be-SU-chen)
  • verstehen: Verstehst du das?
  • bekommen: Ich bekomme einen Brief. ("I get a letter", not "I become"!)
  • erzählen: Er erzählt eine Geschichte. ("He tells a story.")
  • vergessen: Vergiss deinen Schlüssel nicht!
  • beginnen, bezahlen, verkaufen, empfehlen (to recommend), gehören (to belong).

The stress is a reliable guide: a stressed prefix separates (ANrufen → ich rufe an); an unstressed prefix does not (beSUchen → ich besuche).

Worked example: a separable verb in four sentences

Use einkaufen ("to go shopping") in four kinds of sentence.

  1. Statement, verb in position 2, prefix at the end: Ich kaufe heute ein.
  2. Starting with a time, the verb stays second: Am Samstag kauft Jonas im Supermarkt ein.
  3. With a modal verb, one word at the end: Wir müssen noch einkaufen.
  4. Imperative to a friend: Kauf bitte Milch ein!

docs.title: 13.4 Grammar: reflexive verbs and the order of events
Reflexive verbs and pronouns
docs.text:
A reflexive verb has an object that refers back to the subject, like English I hurt myself. German has many more of these verbs than English: sich anziehen ("to get dressed", literally "to dress oneself"), sich beeilen ("to hurry"), sich freuen ("to be glad"). The reflexive pronouns are the accusative pronouns of Lesson 8, except in the third person and the polite form, which all use sich:

Person Reflexive pronoun sich anziehen ich mich ich ziehe mich an du dich du ziehst dich an er, sie, es sich er zieht sich an wir uns wir ziehen uns an ihr euch ihr zieht euch an sie, Sie sich sie ziehen sich an

Table 13.5. The reflexive pronouns. sich is never written with a capital, even for Sie: Setzen Sie sich!

The reflexive pronoun goes straight after the conjugated verb, or after the subject if the subject follows the verb:

  • Ich beeile mich.
  • Morgens ziehe ich mich schnell an.
  • Freust du dich?
  • Ich muss mich beeilen.

In the imperative: Beeil dich! Beeilt euch! Beeilen Sie sich!

Some reflexive verbs are only reflexive (sich beeilen); others can also take an ordinary object: Ich wasche mich ("I wash myself") but Ich wasche das Auto ("I wash the car"). With a part of the body or clothes, German uses a dative reflexive pronoun, mir or dir, and the definite article: Ich putze mir die Zähne. ("I brush my teeth.") Ich wasche mir die Hände. ("I wash my hands.") Learn these as phrases.

sich treffen and sich freuen

sich treffen means "to meet (each other)": Wir treffen uns um sieben. Without sich, treffen takes an object: Ich treffe Ravi. sich freuen means "to be glad": Ich freue mich! With auf + accusative it means "to look forward to": Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende.

docs.title: Telling the order of events
docs.text:
To describe a routine, link the steps with zuerst, dann, danach, später, zum Schluss. Each of them takes position 1, so the verb comes next and the subject follows it (Lesson 7):

  • Zuerst dusche ich.
  • Dann ziehe ich mich an.
  • Danach frühstücke ich.
  • Um halb acht gehe ich los.
  • Zum Schluss sehe ich ein bisschen fern.

docs.title: How often?
docs.text:
Frequency words usually come after the verb and the subject, or in position 1: Ich frühstücke immer. Ich sehe selten fern. Normalerweise stehe ich um neun auf.

erst with a time means "not until", and schon means "already": Ich stehe erst um neun auf. ("I don't get up until nine.") Emma ist schon wach. ("Emma is already awake.")

Figure 13.2 Emma's day. A timeline of Emma's weekday from 6.30 in the morning to 11 at night, with the verbs placed at their times: 6.30 sie steht auf; 6.40 sie duscht sich und zieht sich an; 7.00 sie frühstückt; 7.30 sie geht los; 8.00 der Kurs fängt an; 13.00 sie kommt nach Hause; 15.00 sie kauft ein; 19.00 sie kocht; 21.00 sie sieht fern; 23.00 sie schläft ein.

docs.text:
Infinitive er form in a sentence aufräumen Er räumt sein Zimmer auf. besuchen Er besucht seine Oma. anrufen Er ruft seine Schwester an. verstehen Er versteht alles. einladen Er lädt uns ein. bekommen Er bekommt ein Geschenk. fernsehen Er sieht abends fern.

docs.text:

docs.title: Jonas's Saturday
docs.text:
Read aloud.

  • Am Samstag wacht Jonas erst um zehn auf. — On Saturday Jonas doesn't wake up until ten.
  • Zuerst trinkt er einen Kaffee, dann duscht er. — First he drinks a coffee, then he has a shower.
  • Mittags arbeitet er im Café. — At midday he works in the café.
  • Um fünf kommt er zurück und ruht sich aus. — At five he comes back and rests.
  • Abends gehen er und seine Freunde aus. — In the evening he and his friends go out.
  • Er kommt oft erst um zwei Uhr nachts nach Hause. — He often doesn't get home until two in the morning.

Say it

Describe your weekday in eight sentences, from getting up to going to sleep. Use at least four separable verbs, two reflexive verbs, and zuerst, dann, danach, zum Schluss. For example:

Ich wache um sieben auf. Zuerst dusche ich, dann ziehe ich mich an. Danach frühstücke ich. Um acht gehe ich los. Die Arbeit fängt um neun an. Abends kaufe ich ein und sehe fern. Zum Schluss lese ich ein bisschen und schlafe ein.

docs.title: 13.6 Culture: the rhythm of the day
docs.text:
Early starts. The day starts early in the German-speaking countries. Schools often begin at about eight, or even earlier, and many offices and shops open at eight or nine; tradespeople may start work at seven. In return, many people finish work in the late afternoon and enjoy their Feierabend, the free time after work, a word with no exact English equivalent. Schönen Feierabend! is a friendly way to say goodbye to colleagues at the end of the day.

Meals. Breakfast (das Frühstück) is usually bread or rolls with butter, jam, honey, cheese or cold meats, or muesli, with coffee or tea; at weekends it may be a long, leisurely affair. Many people have a mid-morning snack, which has a different name in each region: die Brotzeit in Bavaria, die Jause in Austria, and in Switzerland das Znüni (from "at nine") in the morning and das Zvieri (from "at four") in the afternoon. Traditionally the hot main meal was lunch (das Mittagessen), and the evening meal was a simple, cold Abendbrot, "evening bread", with bread, cheese, cold meats and salad. Today many working people eat a light lunch and cook in the evening, but the tradition of the cold supper is still alive.

Mahlzeit! In many workplaces, especially in Germany and Austria, colleagues greet each other around lunchtime with Mahlzeit! ("mealtime!"), whether or not they are eating. Some people love the custom and others find it old-fashioned, but you will certainly hear it.

School and childcare. In Germany, schools traditionally ended at lunchtime, and children ate lunch at home. All-day schools (die Ganztagsschule) are now increasingly common, but in many places the school day still ends in the early afternoon.

docs.title: 13.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Separable verbs: stressed prefix (ab-, an-, auf-, aus-, ein-, fern-, los-, mit-, vorbei-, zu-, zurück-) goes to the end when the verb is in position 2 or 1: Ich stehe um sieben auf. Kommst du mit? Ruf mich an!
  • With a modal verb the infinitive stays in one piece at the end: Ich muss früh aufstehen.
  • Inseparable prefixes: be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss-, ver-, zer-, unstressed: besuchen, verstehen, bekommen (= get).
  • Reflexive pronouns: mich, dich, sich, uns, euch, sich: Ich ziehe mich an. Beeil dich! Setzen Sie sich! Body parts: Ich putze mir die Zähne.
  • Order of events: zuerst, dann, danach, später, zum Schluss in position 1, verb next.
  • Frequency: immer, meistens, oft, manchmal, selten, nie; erst um neun = not until nine.

docs.title: Lesson 9: Family and Describing People
docs.text:
Die Familie und Personen beschreiben

Talking about your family is one of the first real conversations you have in a new language: who is in the photo, how old your sister is, what your parents do, what your best friend is like. In this lesson you learn the words for family members, for what people look like and for what they are like, and the grammar you need to talk about them: the possessives for every person (his, her, our, their), the ways of saying Jonas's sister, adjectives after sein, and comparisons such as older than and as tall as.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • name the members of your family and say how they are related to you;
  • use the possessives mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, ihr, Ihr in the nominative and accusative;
  • say whose something is: Jonas' Schwester, Emmas Bruder, die Schwester von Jonas;
  • describe what people look like and what they are like, with sehr, ziemlich, ein bisschen and zu;
  • compare people with älter als, so groß wie and am größten;
  • talk about a family photo.

masculinefeminineneuterplural

docs.title: 9.1 Dialogue: the family photo
docs.text:
Jonas's cousin Sophie has come from Vienna for the weekend. Jonas shows Emma a family photo.

  • Sophie: Servus, Emma! Ich bin Sophie, die Cousine von Jonas. — Hi, Emma! I'm Sophie, Jonas's cousin.
  • Emma: Hallo, Sophie! Freut mich. Du wohnst in Wien, oder? — Hi, Sophie! Nice to meet you. You live in Vienna, don't you?
  • Sophie: Ja, genau. Mein Vater ist Österreicher, und meine Mutter ist die Schwester von Jonas' Vater. — Yes, exactly. My father is Austrian, and my mother is the sister of Jonas's father.
  • Emma: Jonas, ist das deine Familie? — Jonas, is this your family?
  • Jonas: Ja. Das sind meine Eltern, Thomas und Petra. Mein Vater ist Ingenieur, und meine Mutter ist Lehrerin. — Yes. These are my parents, Thomas and Petra. My father is an engineer, and my mother is a teacher.
  • Emma: Und wer ist der Mann hier, mit dem Bart? — And who is the man here, with the beard?
  • Jonas: Das ist mein Onkel Stefan, Sophies Vater. Er ist sehr lustig. — That's my uncle Stefan, Sophie's father. He's very funny.
  • Sophie: Ja, mein Vater ist lustig, aber auch ziemlich laut! — Yes, my father is funny, but also quite loud!
  • Emma: Und die Frau neben ihm? Sie hat lange, rote Haare. — And the woman next to him? She has long red hair.
  • Sophie: Das ist meine Mutter, Karin. Und das hier bin ich, mit zehn. — That's my mother, Karin. And this is me, at ten.
  • Emma: Und das Baby? — And the baby?
  • Jonas: Das bin ich! Und das sind meine Geschwister, Lena und Tim. Sie sind beide älter als ich. Ich bin am jüngsten. — That's me! And these are my brother and sister, Lena and Tim. They're both older than me. I'm the youngest.
  • Emma: Hast du auch Geschwister, Sophie? — Do you have brothers and sisters too, Sophie?
  • Sophie: Nein, ich bin Einzelkind. Aber Jonas ist wie ein Bruder für mich. Und deine Familie, Emma? — No, I'm an only child. But Jonas is like a brother to me. And your family, Emma?
  • Emma: Ich habe einen Bruder, Oliver. Er ist groß und schlank und hat kurze, blonde Haare. Er ist sehr sportlich, aber ein bisschen schüchtern. Er ist verheiratet, und seine Frau heißt Aisha. — I have a brother, Oliver. He's tall and slim and has short blond hair. He's very sporty, but a bit shy. He's married, and his wife's name is Aisha.

Notice:

  1. "His" is sein and "her" is ihr, and they take endings like mein: seine Frau, ihr Vater.
  2. "Sophie's father" is Sophies Vater, with an s and no apostrophe; "Jonas's father" is Jonas' Vater, with only an apostrophe; and in speech, der Vater von Jonas.
  3. Adjectives after sein have no ending: Er ist lustig. Er ist groß und schlank.
  4. "Older than" is älter als; "the youngest" is am jüngsten.

docs.title: The family
docs.text:

docs.text:
German English groß / klein tall / short (small) schlank slim jung / alt young / old hübsch pretty, good-looking gut aussehend handsome, good-looking Er hat kurze Haare. He has short hair. Sie hat lange, blonde Haare. She has long blond hair. braune, schwarze, graue, rote Haare brown, black, grey, red hair Er hat blaue Augen. He has blue eyes. braune, grüne, graue Augen brown, green, grey eyes Er hat einen Bart. He has a beard. Sie trägt eine Brille. She wears glasses.

docs.title: What people are like
docs.text:
German English German English nett, freundlich nice, friendly unfreundlich unfriendly sympathisch likeable, pleasant unsympathisch unpleasant lustig funny, cheerful ernst serious ruhig quiet, calm laut loud fleißig hard-working faul lazy geduldig patient ungeduldig impatient klug, intelligent clever, intelligent schüchtern shy sportlich sporty kreativ creative ehrlich honest hilfsbereit helpful

Table 9.3. Character. The prefix un- makes many adjectives negative, as in English.

False friends: sympathisch and eventuell

sympathisch does not mean "sympathetic" (understanding someone's troubles, which is mitfühlend or verständnisvoll). It means "likeable, pleasant": Dein Bruder ist sehr sympathisch. is a compliment. Words that look like English but mean something different are called false friends; the Review lesson collects the most common ones.

docs.title: The possessives for every person
docs.text:
Each personal pronoun has a possessive. All of them take the same endings as ein and mein (Lessons 5 and 8).

Pronoun Possessive English Example ich mein my mein Vater, meine Mutter du dein your dein Vater, deine Mutter er sein his sein Vater, seine Mutter sie ihr her ihr Vater, ihre Mutter es sein its sein Vater, seine Mutter wir unser our unser Vater, unsere Mutter ihr euer your (plural) euer Vater, eure Mutter sie ihr their ihr Vater, ihre Mutter Sie Ihr your (polite) Ihr Vater, Ihre Mutter

Table 9.4. The possessives. euer loses its second e when an ending is added: eure, euren.

docs.title: Two decisions: which word, and which ending
docs.text:
Choosing a possessive takes two steps, and English speakers often mix them up:

  1. The owner decides the word. If the owner is a man or a masculine noun, use sein; if a woman, a feminine noun or a group, use ihr. This is the same as English his and her.

  2. The noun that follows decides the ending. sein and ihr take the endings of ein, according to the gender, number and case of the thing owned.

  3. Jonas and his sister: Jonas und seine Schwester (owner a man → sein; Schwester feminine → -e).

  4. Lena and her brother: Lena und ihr Bruder (owner a woman → ihr; Bruder masculine nominative → no ending).
  5. Lena visits her brother: Lena besucht ihren Bruder (accusative masculine → -en).
  6. Emma and Oliver visit their parents: Emma und Oliver besuchen ihre Eltern (owner a group → ihr; plural → -e).
Case Masculine Feminine Neuter Plural nominative unser Sohn unsere Tochter unser Kind unsere Kinder accusative unseren Sohn unsere Tochter unser Kind unsere Kinder nominative ihr Sohn ihre Tochter ihr Kind ihre Kinder accusative ihren Sohn ihre Tochter ihr Kind ihre Kinder

Table 9.5. Possessive endings: the same as ein (and keine in the plural).

Common mistake: sein and ihr

In some languages, the word for "his" or "her" agrees only with the thing owned, so French sa mère can be "his mother" or "her mother". German, like English, also looks at the owner. "Lena and her father" is Lena und ihr Vater, never Lena und sein Vater, even though Vater is masculine. The ending looks at Vater; the word looks at Lena.

docs.title: Whose? Names with s, and von
docs.text:
To say whose something is with a name, German adds -s to the name, without an apostrophe, and puts it before the noun:

  • Sophies Vater — Sophie's father
  • Emmas Bruder — Emma's brother
  • Frau Wagners Kurs — Frau Wagner's course

When the name already ends in an s sound (-s, -ß, -x, -z), only an apostrophe is written: Jonas' Vater, Max' Schwester.

In speech, and with nouns that are not names, the most common way is von ("of, from") + the owner: die Schwester von Jonas, der Vater von Sophie, das Auto von meinem Bruder. After von, an article is in the dative (von meinem Bruder, von meiner Schwester), which Lesson 11 explains. With names, it needs no endings at all.

In writing you will also meet the genitive case, with des and der: das Auto meines Bruders ("my brother's car"), die Wohnung meiner Schwester. Learn to recognise it; at this level you can always use von instead.

docs.title: Adjectives after sein
docs.text:
An adjective that comes after sein (or werden) has no ending, whatever the gender or number of the noun:

  • Mein Onkel ist lustig. Meine Tante ist lustig. Das Kind ist lustig. Meine Cousins sind lustig.

An adjective before a noun takes an ending: ein lustiger Onkel, eine lustige Tante. The full system of adjective endings is a subject for the next stage of your German; for now, use adjectives after sein, and learn two useful patterns as they are:

  • Plural noun without an article: adjective + -e. Sie hat lange Haare. Er hat blaue Augen. Ich habe nette Kollegen. This covers hair and eyes.
  • Two adjectives before a noun are separated by a comma, and both take the same ending: kurze, blonde Haare.

docs.title: Sehr, ziemlich, ein bisschen, zu
docs.text:
These words make an adjective stronger or weaker. They come before it:

German English Example sehr very Er ist sehr nett. ziemlich quite, rather Sie ist ziemlich groß. ein bisschen a bit Er ist ein bisschen schüchtern. nicht so not very Das Baby ist nicht so ruhig. gar nicht not at all Er ist gar nicht faul. zu too Die Musik ist zu laut.

Table 9.6. Words before adjectives. zu ("too") is always critical: zu groß means bigger than it should be.

docs.title: Comparing: older than, as tall as
docs.text:
To compare two people or things, add -er to the adjective and use als ("than"):

  • Lena ist alt. → Lena ist älter als Jonas. — Lena is older than Jonas.
  • Tim ist groß. → Tim ist größer als sein Vater. — Tim is taller than his father.
  • Meine Schwester ist ruhiger als ich. — My sister is quieter than me.

Many short adjectives with a, o, u take an umlaut: alt → älter, jung → jünger, groß → größer, kurz → kürzer, lang → länger. A few are irregular: gut → besser, viel → mehr, gern → lieber.

To say two things are equal, use so … wie ("as … as"): Tim ist so groß wie sein Vater. Ich bin nicht so sportlich wie mein Bruder.

To say who is the most, use am + adjective + -sten (the superlative): Jonas ist am jüngsten. ("Jonas is the youngest.") Lena ist am ältesten. Wer ist am größten? Adjectives ending in -t, -d, -s, -ß, -z add -esten: am ältesten, am kürzesten; but groß gives am größten. Irregular: am besten, am meisten, am liebsten.

Adjective Comparative Superlative klein kleiner am kleinsten alt älter am ältesten jung jünger am jüngsten groß größer am größten gut besser am besten viel mehr am meisten gern lieber am liebsten

Table 9.7. Comparison of adjectives.

Common mistake: more older, als and wie

German never uses a word for "more" with short adjectives: älter, not mehr alt. And even long adjectives take -er: intelligenter, interessanter. Keep als for "than" after a comparative and wie for "as" after so: älter als, so alt wie.

Worked example: describing a person

Describe Lena from these notes: Jonas's sister; 29; doctor in Leipzig; tall, short brown hair, glasses; patient and very hard-working; older than Tim.

  1. Relation, with a possessive: Das ist Lena, die Schwester von Jonas. or Das ist Jonas' Schwester Lena.
  2. Age and job: Sie ist neunundzwanzig und Ärztin in Leipzig.
  3. Looks, with adjectives after sein and the hair pattern: Sie ist groß und hat kurze, braune Haare. Sie trägt eine Brille.
  4. Character, with sehr: Sie ist geduldig und sehr fleißig.
  5. Comparison: Sie ist älter als Tim. (She is in fact the oldest: Sie ist am ältesten.)

docs.title: My family
docs.text:
Read the text aloud, then write a similar text about your own family.

  • Meine Familie ist nicht sehr groß. — My family isn't very big.
  • Mein Vater heißt David und ist Ingenieur. Er ist ruhig und sehr geduldig. — My father is called David and is an engineer. He is quiet and very patient.
  • Meine Mutter heißt Claire. Sie ist Ärztin und ziemlich ernst, aber auch lustig. — My mother is called Claire. She is a doctor and rather serious, but also funny.
  • Mein Bruder Oliver ist drei Jahre älter als ich. — My brother Oliver is three years older than me.
  • Unsere Großeltern wohnen in Schottland. Wir besuchen sie jeden Sommer. — Our grandparents live in Scotland. We visit them every summer.

Say it

Take a photo of your family or friends, or imagine one, and describe three people in it: who they are, how old they are, what they look like and what they are like. Compare two of them. For example:

Das ist meine Schwester. Sie ist fünfundzwanzig. Sie hat lange, schwarze Haare und braune Augen. Sie ist sehr kreativ und ein bisschen laut. Sie ist jünger als ich, aber größer.

docs.title: 9.6 Culture: family life
docs.text:
Grandparents, aunts and Sunday afternoons. Family ties in the German-speaking countries are close, though families today are often small and spread across the country. Grandparents, Oma and Opa, often play an important part in looking after grandchildren. A traditional family occasion is Kaffee und Kuchen on a Sunday afternoon: coffee and homemade cake around three or four o'clock, with grandparents, aunts and uncles. Birthdays, Christmas and Easter are the great family festivals.

Kindergarten. The word kindergarten, "children's garden", is German; it was coined in the nineteenth century by the educator Friedrich Fröbel, who founded the first one. In Germany today, children usually go to a day-care centre, the Kita (short for Kindertagesstätte), and then start school at about six. Parents in Germany and Austria are entitled to paid parental leave, and many fathers take part of it too.

Many kinds of family. As elsewhere in Europe, families take many forms: married and unmarried couples, single parents, same-sex couples (marriage for same-sex couples has been legal in Germany since 2017, in Austria since 2019 and in Switzerland since 2022), and stepfamilies, which are often called Patchworkfamilien, a borrowing from English.

Names. Germans have a first name (der Vorname) and a surname (der Nachname or der Familienname). When a couple marries, they may choose either partner's surname as the family name, keep their own names, or add one name to the other with a hyphen. Many common surnames come from old trades: Müller (miller), Schmidt (smith), Schneider (tailor), Fischer, Weber (weaver), Becker (baker) and Wagner (cartwright).

docs.title: 9.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Family: die Eltern, der Vater, die Mutter, der Sohn, die Tochter, die Geschwister, die Großeltern, der Onkel, die Tante, der Cousin, die Cousine.
  • Possessives: mein, dein, sein, ihr, sein, unser, euer, ihr, Ihr, with the endings of ein: seine Frau, ihren Bruder, eure Eltern.
  • Two decisions: the owner chooses sein (his) or ihr (her, their); the noun chooses the ending.
  • Whose: Sophies Vater (no apostrophe); Jonas' Vater; spoken der Vater von Jonas.
  • Adjectives after sein: no ending. Patterns: Sie hat lange Haare. Er hat blaue Augen.
  • Degree: sehr, ziemlich, ein bisschen, nicht so, gar nicht, zu.
  • Comparison: älter als, so alt wie, am ältesten; umlaut in short adjectives; gut, besser, am besten.

docs.title: 9.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

What is your mother's sister to you?

Answer

Tante. meine Tante, my aunt.

Exercise 2

Complete: Lena und ___ Mann wohnen in Leipzig. (her)

Answer

ihr. Lena und ihr Mann. Owner a woman: ihr; Mann masculine nominative: no ending.

Exercise 3

Complete: Jonas besucht ___ Oma. (his)

Answer

seine. Jonas besucht seine Oma.

Exercise 4

Complete: Wir lieben ___ Hund. (our)

Answer

unseren. Wir lieben unseren Hund. Accusative masculine: -en.

Exercise 5

Write "Anna's brother" in the written form with s.

Answer

Annas Bruder. Annas Bruder, without an apostrophe.

Exercise 6

Give the comparative of jung.

Answer

jünger. jünger, with an umlaut.

Exercise 7

Complete: Mein Bruder ist so groß ___ mein Vater.

Answer

wie. so groß wie: as tall as.

Exercise 8

Translate: "She has short black hair and green eyes."

Answer

Sie hat kurze, schwarze Haare und grüne Augen.

Exercise 9

Correct the mistakes: Sophie und sein Vater wohnen in Wien. Ihr Vater ist mehr alt als ihre Mutter.

Answer

Sophie und ihr Vater wohnen in Wien. Ihr Vater ist älter als ihre Mutter. The owner is Sophie, so ihr; the comparative is älter.

Exercise 10

Write four sentences about Jonas's family from Figure 9.1: who Thomas is, who Karin is, who Sophie's parents are, and who is the youngest.

Answer

Thomas ist der Vater von Jonas. Karin ist seine Tante. Sophies Eltern heißen Karin und Stefan. Jonas ist am jüngsten. (Other correct versions are possible, for example Karin ist die Schwester von Thomas.)

docs.title: 9.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: family and describing people

Exercise 11

Der Sohn von meinem Onkel ist mein ___.

  1. Neffe
  2. Cousin
  3. Enkel
  4. Bruder
Answer

Cousin

Exercise 12

Lena besucht ___ Vater.

  1. sein
  2. seinen
  3. ihr
  4. ihren
Answer

The owner is Lena, so ihr; Vater is a masculine object, so -en.

Exercise 13

Mein Bruder ist drei Jahre ___ als ich. (alt)

Answer

älter / aelter

Exercise 14

Jonas ist ___ jüngsten.

Answer

am

Exercise 15

Match the opposites.

ABfleißigkleinlauternstgroßfaullustigruhig Answer

fleißig — faul; laut — ruhig; groß — klein; lustig — ernst

Exercise 16

Write "Sophie's mother" in German, with s.

Answer

Sophies Mutter

Exercise 17

Tap the wrong word.

Meine Schwester ist mehr sportlich als ich.

Answer

Wrong word: mehr.

Corrected: Meine Schwester ist sportlicher als ich.

German adds -er to the adjective instead of using mehr.

Exercise 18

Put the words in order: "He has short blond hair."

Words: hat / Haare. / blonde / Er / kurze,

Answer

Er hat kurze, blonde Haare.

Exercise 19

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Meine Eltern wohnen in Dresden.

Answer

Meine Eltern wohnen in Dresden.

docs.title: Lesson 10: Food and Shopping
docs.text:
Essen, Trinken und Einkaufen

Buying food is where a new language meets daily life: at the bakery counter, at the market, in the café. The good news is that the language of these situations is short and predictable. The seller asks Was darf es sein? ("What would you like?"), you ask for what you want politely, they ask Sonst noch etwas? ("Anything else?"), and you pay. In this lesson you learn the words for food and drink, quantities and prices, the polite ways of asking for things with ich möchte and ich hätte gern, and the imperative, the form of the verb for instructions, invitations and requests.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • name common foods and drinks, with their genders and plurals;
  • buy food in a shop or market: ask for quantities, ask the price, and pay;
  • order and pay in a café or restaurant, separately or together, with a tip;
  • ask politely with ich möchte, ich hätte gern and ich nehme;
  • use noch ein ("another") and kein … mehr ("no more");
  • give instructions and make requests with the imperative for Sie, du and ihr.

masculinefeminineneuterplural

docs.title: 10.1 Dialogue: at the bakery and in the café
At the bakery
docs.text:
On Saturday morning, Emma buys breakfast.

  • Verkäuferin: Guten Morgen! Was darf es sein? — Good morning! What would you like?
  • Emma: Guten Morgen! Ich hätte gern vier Brötchen und ein Vollkornbrot, bitte. — Good morning! I'd like four rolls and a wholemeal loaf, please.
  • Verkäuferin: Gern. Sonst noch etwas? — Certainly. Anything else?
  • Emma: Ja, zwei Stück Apfelkuchen, bitte. — Yes, two pieces of apple cake, please.
  • Verkäuferin: Mit Sahne? — With cream?
  • Emma: Nein, danke, ohne Sahne. Was macht das? — No, thanks, without cream. How much is that?
  • Verkäuferin: Das macht neun Euro vierzig. — That's nine euros forty.
  • Emma: Hier sind zehn Euro. — Here's ten euros.
  • Verkäuferin: Und sechzig Cent zurück. Schönes Wochenende! — And sixty cents change. Have a nice weekend!

docs.title: In the café
docs.text:
At lunchtime, Emma and Ravi go to a café.

  • Kellner: Guten Tag! Was möchten Sie trinken? — Hello! What would you like to drink?
  • Ravi: Ich nehme einen Cappuccino, bitte. — I'll have a cappuccino, please.
  • Emma: Und für mich einen Tee mit Milch, bitte. — And a tea with milk for me, please.
  • Kellner: Möchten Sie auch etwas essen? — Would you like something to eat as well?
  • Ravi: Ja. Ist Fleisch in der Kartoffelsuppe? Ich esse kein Fleisch. — Yes. Is there meat in the potato soup? I don't eat meat.
  • Kellner: Nein, die Suppe ist vegetarisch. — No, the soup is vegetarian.
  • Ravi: Gut, dann nehme ich die Suppe. — Good, then I'll have the soup.
  • Emma: Und ich hätte gern die Käsespätzle. — And I'd like the cheese noodles.
  • (Later)
  • Emma: Entschuldigung, wir möchten zahlen, bitte! — Excuse me, we'd like to pay, please!
  • Kellner: Zusammen oder getrennt? — Together or separately?
  • Ravi: Getrennt, bitte. — Separately, please.
  • Kellner: Der Cappuccino und die Suppe: elf Euro achtzig. — The cappuccino and the soup: eleven euros eighty.
  • Ravi: Machen Sie dreizehn. — Make it thirteen.
  • Kellner: Danke schön! Und für Sie? — Thank you! And for you?
  • Emma: Der Tee und die Käsespätzle. — The tea and the cheese noodles.
  • Kellner: Das macht vierzehn Euro zwanzig. — That's fourteen euros twenty.
  • Emma: Fünfzehn, bitte. Stimmt so. — Fifteen, please. Keep the change.

Notice:

  1. To ask for something politely, say Ich hätte gern …, Ich möchte … or Ich nehme …. What you ask for is an object in the accusative: einen Cappuccino, einen Tee.
  2. Quantities need no word for "of": zwei Stück Apfelkuchen, "two pieces (of) apple cake".
  3. When you pay, you can include the tip by saying the total you want to pay: Machen Sie dreizehn, or say Stimmt so ("that's right as it is") when you hand over the money.
  4. Machen Sie dreizehn is an imperative: an instruction or request.
