docs.title: People
docs.text:
Singular Plural English der Mann die Männer the man die Frau die Frauen the woman das Kind die Kinder the child der Junge die Jungen the boy das Mädchen die Mädchen the girl der Lehrer / die Lehrerin die Lehrer / die Lehrerinnen the teacher (man / woman) der Student / die Studentin die Studenten / die Studentinnen the student der Freund / die Freundin die Freunde / die Freundinnen the friend; also boyfriend / girlfriend

Table 4.3. People. Most words for people have a feminine form in -in.

Learn the noun with its article, and use the colours

Never learn Tisch on its own: learn der Tisch, plural die Tische. Make flashcards in three colours, one for each gender, as this book does, or picture masculine nouns in one room of an imaginary house, feminine nouns in another and neuter nouns in a third. The article is part of the word; without it you will be guessing for years.

docs.title: Three genders
docs.text:
German has three definite articles in the singular, one for each gender, and one in the plural:

Masculine Feminine Neuter Plural "the" der Tisch die Lampe das Bett die Tische pronoun er sie es sie

Table 4.4. The definite article and the matching pronoun. Switch on Practice and fill them in.

For people, the grammatical gender usually follows the person: der Mann, der Vater, die Frau, die Mutter. For things and ideas there is no logic in the meaning: der Löffel (spoon), die Gabel (fork) and das Messer (knife) are one of each. But the form of a noun, and especially its ending, often shows the gender. The rules below cover a large part of everyday vocabulary.

docs.title: Masculine: der
docs.text:
• Male people and animals: der Mann, der Vater, der Sohn, der Onkel.
  • Days, months, seasons: der Montag, der Mai, der Sommer (Lesson 3).
  • Weather and points of the compass: der Regen, der Schnee, der Wind, der Norden, der Süden.
  • Nouns in -er made from verbs, for people and machines: der Lehrer (from lehren, to teach), der Fernseher, der Computer.
  • The endings -ling, -ismus, -ist: der Frühling, der Tourismus, der Tourist.

docs.title: Feminine: die
docs.text:
• Female people and animals: die Frau, die Mutter, die Tochter, die Tante, and the feminine forms in -in: die Lehrerin, die Studentin, die Ärztin.
  • Most nouns ending in -e: die Lampe, die Küche, die Tasche, die Straße, die Woche. This is a strong tendency, not a law (see the exceptions below), but it is right far more often than not.
  • The endings -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft: die Wohnung, die Zeitung, die Freiheit, die Möglichkeit, die Freundschaft. These are completely reliable.
  • The endings -ion, -tät, -ik, -ie, -ei, -ur: die Information, die Universität, die Musik, die Familie, die Bäckerei, die Kultur. Most of them correspond to English words, which makes them easy to spot.

docs.title: Neuter: das
docs.text:
• The endings -chen and -lein, which make "little" words, always neuter: das Mädchen (girl, originally "little maid"), das Brötchen (bread roll, "little bread"), das Häuschen (little house).
  • Young people and animals: das Kind, das Baby.
  • Infinitives used as nouns: das Essen (food, eating), das Leben (life), das Schwimmen (swimming).
  • The endings -um and -ment, in words from Latin: das Museum, das Zentrum, das Datum, das Dokument, das Instrument.
  • Many short words borrowed from other languages: das Hotel, das Kino, das Café, das Restaurant, das Auto, das Büro, das Handy, das Sofa.
  • Colours and languages used as nouns: das Rot, das Deutsch.
Figure 4.1 Clues to the gender. A chart in three columns. The blue masculine column, headed "der", lists male people, days, months and seasons, weather, nouns in -er from verbs, and the endings -ling and -ismus, with the examples der Vater, der Montag, der Regen, der Lehrer, der Frühling. The pink feminine column, headed "die", lists female people and -in, most nouns in -e, and the endings -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -tät, -ik, -ie, with the examples die Mutter, die Lampe, die Wohnung, die Information, die Musik. The grey neuter column, headed "das", lists -chen and -lein, young beings, infinitives as nouns, -um and -ment, and many borrowed words, with the examples das Mädchen, das Kind, das Essen, das Museum, das Hotel. A box below says: compounds take the gender of the last part, das Haus plus die Tür gives die Haustür.

docs.title: The exceptions to learn now
docs.text:
Word Why it is surprising das Mädchen a girl, but -chen is always neuter der Junge ends in -e, but a male person der Name ends in -e, but masculine der Käse ends in -e, but masculine das Ende ends in -e, but neuter das Auge ends in -e, but neuter (the eye) das Bier most alcoholic drinks are masculine (der Wein), but beer is neuter

Table 4.5. Common exceptions.

Das Mädchen: es or sie?

Strictly, a pronoun follows the grammatical gender, so das Mädchen is es: Das Mädchen heißt Lea. Es ist sieben. In everyday speech, though, people often switch to sie when they go on talking about the girl, especially in a longer text. Both are heard; at this stage, use es straight after the noun.

docs.title: The pronouns er, sie, es for things
docs.text:
Because every noun has a gender, "it" has three forms in German. A thing is referred to with the pronoun of its gender:

  • Wo ist der Schlüssel? – Er ist hier. — Where is the key? – It is here.
  • Wie ist die Küche? – Sie ist groß. — What is the kitchen like? – It is big.
  • Ist das Zimmer klein? – Ja, es ist klein. — Is the room small? – Yes, it is small.
  • Wo sind die Bücher? – Sie sind im Regal. — Where are the books? – They are on the shelf.

The trick is that er looks like der, sie like die, and es like das: the last letter of the article is the pronoun's clue (der → er, das → es).

Common mistake: es for everything

English speakers tend to say es for every thing, because English says it. Der Tisch ist neu. Es ist schön. is wrong: the table is masculine, so Er ist schön. Always look back at the article.

docs.title: The plural article
docs.text: In the plural there is only one article for all three genders, die, and one pronoun, sie (they). The plural is easy to recognise but harder to form, because the noun itself changes in one of several ways.

docs.title: The plural patterns
docs.text:
Pattern Singular Plural Typical for -e der Tisch, das Heft die Tische, die Hefte many short masculine and neuter nouns umlaut + -e der Stuhl, die Stadt die Stühle, die Städte many short masculine nouns, some feminine (umlaut +) -er das Kind, das Buch die Kinder, die Bücher many short neuter nouns; umlaut where possible -n / -en die Lampe, die Frau die Lampen, die Frauen almost all feminine nouns -nen die Lehrerin die Lehrerinnen feminine nouns in -in no ending der Lehrer, das Zimmer die Lehrer, die Zimmer masculine and neuter nouns in -er, -el, -en, -chen, -lein umlaut only der Vater, die Mutter die Väter, die Mütter a few common nouns, many of them family words -s das Auto, das Handy die Autos, die Handys words ending in a vowel other than -e; many borrowed words

Table 4.6. The plural patterns. The bold letters show what changes.

The column "Typical for" gives you rules of thumb that work most of the time:

  1. Feminine nouns almost all add -n or -en: die Lampen, die Wohnungen, die Türen, die Zeitungen. Learn the few exceptions as you meet them: die Städte, die Hände, die Nächte, die Mütter, die Töchter.
  2. Masculine and neuter nouns ending in -er, -el, -en, -chen, -lein add nothing, though some take an umlaut: die Fenster, die Schlüssel, die Mädchen; die Väter, die Äpfel, die Gärten.
  3. Short masculine nouns usually add -e, often with an umlaut: die Tage, die Freunde, die Stühle, die Schränke.
  4. Short neuter nouns add -e or -er: die Hefte, die Jahre; die Kinder, die Bilder, die Bücher, die Häuser.
  5. Words ending in -a, -i, -o, -u, -y and many recent borrowings add -s: die Sofas, die Kulis, die Kinos, die Handys, die Hotels.

Even native speakers learnt the plurals one by one, as children. Take the same path: learn the plural with the noun, and these rules will make most of them feel natural.

Common mistake: adding -s to everything

English makes almost every plural with -s, so English speakers are tempted to do the same in German. Only a minority of German nouns take -s. die Tischs and die Lampes are wrong: die Tische, die Lampen.

docs.title: Nouns with no singular or no plural
docs.text:
Some nouns are plural in German where English uses a singular, and the other way round:

  • die Brille is one pair of glasses, singular: Die Brille ist neu. So is die Hose, a pair of trousers.
  • die Eltern (the parents) and die Leute (the people) exist only in the plural.
  • die Information has a plural, die Informationen, used where English says information without a plural.

docs.title: Compound nouns
docs.text:
German freely joins nouns together into one long word, the compound noun (das Kompositum). English does the same with bedroom or toothbrush, but usually writes the parts apart (front door, washing machine). Two rules make compounds easy:

  1. The last part says what the thing is, and gives the gender and the plural of the whole word. The parts before it describe it.
  2. The main stress falls on the first part.
Parts Compound English das Haus + die Tür die Haustür the front door kühl + der Schrank der Kühlschrank the fridge schlafen + das Zimmer das Schlafzimmer the bedroom das Telefon + die Nummer die Telefonnummer the phone number die Wohnung + die Tür die Wohnungstür the door of the flat der Geburtstag + die Party die Geburtstagsparty the birthday party

Table 4.7. Compound nouns. The article of the compound is the article of its last part.

Sometimes a linking -s- or -n- joins the parts: Wohnung-s-tür, Geburtstag-s-party, Straße-n-bahn (tram). After -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft and -ion there is always an -s-.

Worked example: an unknown compound

You see the word Kinderzimmerlampe. What is it, and what is its article and plural?

  1. Split it from the end: Kinder + Zimmer + Lampe.
  2. The last part says what it is: a lamp. Kinderzimmer (children's room) describes which lamp.
  3. The gender and plural come from die Lampe, plural die Lampen.

So: die Kinderzimmerlampe, the lamp in the children's room; plural die Kinderzimmerlampen. The stress is on the first part: KIN-der-tsim-muh-lahm-puh.

docs.title: Der, die or das?
docs.text:
Use the rules of section 4.3, then check.

Noun With its article Clue Zeitung (newspaper) die Zeitung -ung Brötchen (roll) das Brötchen -chen Winter der Winter season Universität die Universität -tät Museum das Museum -um Straße (street) die Straße -e Tourismus der Tourismus -ismus Kino (cinema) das Kino borrowed, -o Freiheit (freedom) die Freiheit -heit Name der Name exception

Table 4.8. Practice: der, die or das?

docs.title: Plurals
docs.text:
Singular Plural der Stuhl die Stühle die Tür die Türen das Buch die Bücher das Fenster die Fenster das Handy die Handys die Freundin die Freundinnen der Vater die Väter das Haus die Häuser

Table 4.9. Practice: plurals.

docs.title: Where is it?
docs.text:
Answer each question with the right pronoun, as in the model.

  • Wo ist der Kuli? – Er ist hier. — Where is the pen? – It's here.
  • Wo ist die Brille? – Sie ist hier. — Where are the glasses? – They're here.
  • Wo ist das Handy? – Es ist hier. — Where is the phone? – It's here.
  • Wo sind die Schlüssel? – Sie sind hier. — Where are the keys? – They're here.

Say it

Look around the room you are in and name ten things with their articles, then their plurals: der Tisch, die Tische; die Lampe, die Lampen; das Fenster, die Fenster … Then describe three of them with a pronoun: Der Tisch ist alt. Er ist groß.

docs.title: 4.6 Culture: living in Germany, Austria and Switzerland
docs.text:
Renting is normal. In the German-speaking countries, and in Switzerland and Germany above all, far more people rent their homes than in Britain or the United States. Renting a flat for many years, even for life, is common, and tenants are well protected by law. Flats are described by the number of rooms, not bedrooms: a Dreizimmerwohnung (three-room flat) has three rooms plus kitchen and bathroom, and its size is always given in square metres. The rent is quoted as Kaltmiete ("cold rent", the flat alone) or Warmmiete ("warm rent", including heating and other running costs).

The kitchen may not be included. A surprise for many newcomers to Germany is that an unfurnished flat may come without a fitted kitchen: no cupboards, no cooker, sometimes not even a sink. Tenants often buy a kitchen and take it with them, or sell it to the next tenant, when they move.

The WG. Students and young people often share a flat in a Wohngemeinschaft, usually shortened to WG [vay-GAY]. Each person has a room of their own and shares the kitchen and bathroom, as Emma and Jonas do. Advertisements for rooms ask for a Mitbewohner or Mitbewohnerin (flatmate), and new flatmates are often chosen at a casual interview over coffee, the WG-Casting.

Rules of the house. Blocks of flats usually have a set of house rules (die Hausordnung), which may set quiet hours at night and on Sundays and say who cleans the stairs. Rubbish is sorted carefully into several bins: paper, packaging, glass by colour, organic waste and the rest. The colours of the bins and the exact rules vary from town to town, so newcomers ask their neighbours or read the local guide.

docs.title: 4.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Three genders: der (masculine), die (feminine), das (neuter); plural die for all. Pronouns: er, sie, es; plural sie.
  • Masculine: male people, days, months, seasons, weather, -er from verbs, -ling, -ismus.
  • Feminine: female people, -in, most nouns in -e, -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -tät, -ik, -ie.
  • Neuter: -chen, -lein, young beings, infinitives as nouns, -um, -ment, many borrowed words.
  • Exceptions: das Mädchen, der Junge, der Name, der Käse, das Auge, das Ende, das Bier.
  • Plurals: -e (Tische), ¨-e (Stühle), ¨-er (Bücher), -(e)n (Lampen, almost all feminines), -nen (Lehrerinnen), no ending (Zimmer), umlaut (Väter), -s (Autos).
  • Compounds: the last part gives the gender and plural; the first part takes the stress: die Haustür.
  • Learn every noun as article + noun + plural.

docs.title: 4.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Give the definite article: ___ Wohnung.

Answer

die. die Wohnung. Nouns in -ung are always feminine.

Exercise 2

Give the definite article: ___ Mädchen.

Answer

das. das Mädchen. Nouns in -chen are always neuter, even for a girl.

Exercise 3

Give the definite article: ___ Montag.

Answer

der. der Montag. Days of the week are masculine.

Exercise 4

Give the plural: das Kind.

Answer

die Kinder. die Kinder.

Exercise 5

Give the plural: die Lampe.

Answer

die Lampen. die Lampen. Almost all feminine nouns add -n or -en.

Exercise 6

Give the plural: der Schlüssel.

Answer

die Schlüssel. die Schlüssel. Masculine nouns in -el add nothing.

Exercise 7

Complete with a pronoun: Wo ist der Computer? – ___ ist im Büro.

Answer

Er. Er ist im Büro. Der Computer is masculine.

Exercise 8

Give the article of the compound Bahnhofsuhr (station clock), and its plural.

Answer

die Bahnhofsuhr, die Bahnhofsuhren. The last part is die Uhr, plural die Uhren.

Exercise 9

Correct the mistakes: Das Tisch ist neu. Es ist groß. Die Stuhls sind alt.

Answer

Der Tisch ist neu. Er ist groß. Die Stühle sind alt. Tisch is masculine, so der and er; the plural of Stuhl is Stühle.

Exercise 10

Translate: "The bedroom is small, but the windows are big. The books are on the shelf." (on the shelf: im Regal)

Answer

Das Schlafzimmer ist klein, aber die Fenster sind groß. Die Bücher sind im Regal.

docs.title: 4.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: nouns, gender and plurals

Exercise 11

___ Zeitung

  1. der
  2. die
  3. das
Answer

die

-ung is always feminine.

Exercise 12

Which noun is neuter?

  1. Lampe
  2. Brötchen
  3. Montag
  4. Universität
Answer

Brötchen

-chen is always neuter. Lampe and Universität are feminine, Montag masculine.

Exercise 13

das Buch → die ___

Answer

Bücher / Buecher

Exercise 14

Die Lampe ist alt, aber ___ funktioniert.

Answer

sie

die Lampe is feminine, so the pronoun is sie.

Exercise 15

Match each singular to its plural.

ABder Stuhldie Zimmerdie Fraudie Autosdas Zimmerdie Stühledas Autodie Frauen Answer

der Stuhl — die Stühle; die Frau — die Frauen; das Zimmer — die Zimmer; das Auto — die Autos

Exercise 16

Give the article of the compound Haustür.

Answer

die

The last part, die Tür, gives the gender.

Exercise 17

Tap the wrong word.

Der Kühlschrank ist neu. Es ist groß.

Answer

Wrong word: Es.

Corrected: Der Kühlschrank ist neu. Er ist groß.

der Kühlschrank is masculine, so the pronoun is er.

Exercise 18

Put the words in order: "Where are the keys?"

Words: sind / Schlüssel? / die / Wo

Answer

Wo sind die Schlüssel?

Exercise 19

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Das Zimmer ist klein, aber das Fenster ist groß.

Answer

Das Zimmer ist klein, aber das Fenster ist groß.

docs.title: Lesson 3: Numbers, Days, Dates and Time
docs.text:
Zahlen, Tage, Daten und Uhrzeit

Numbers are everywhere in daily life: prices, phone numbers, addresses, ages, the time of the next train. German numbers are logical, but they have one feature that surprises every English speaker: from 21 to 99 the units come first, so 25 is "five-and-twenty", fünfundzwanzig, as in the old English nursery rhyme four-and-twenty blackbirds. German also says "half three" when it means half past two. In this lesson you learn to count, to give prices and phone numbers, to name the days and months, to say dates and birthdays, and to tell the time in the two ways Germans use: the 24-hour clock of timetables and the informal clock of conversation.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • count from 0 to a million, and read prices, phone numbers and years aloud;
  • name the days of the week, the months and the seasons, with am and im;
  • say the date and your birthday with ordinal numbers: am dritten Mai;
  • ask and tell the time, both officially (vierzehn Uhr dreißig) and informally (halb drei);
  • say when something happens with um, am, im and the parts of the day;
  • give your age with Ich bin … Jahre alt.

docs.title: 3.1 Dialogue: a birthday party
docs.text:
Emma and Jonas are having breakfast in the kitchen of their flat.

  • Jonas: Emma, wann hast du Geburtstag? — Emma, when is your birthday?
  • Emma: Am vierzehnten März. Und du? — On the fourteenth of March. And you?
  • Jonas: Am Samstag! Am achtzehnten Oktober. Ich mache eine Party. — On Saturday! On the eighteenth of October. I'm having a party.
  • Emma: Toll! Wie alt bist du dann? — Great! How old will you be then?
  • Jonas: Dreiundzwanzig. Die Party beginnt um acht Uhr abends. Kommst du? — Twenty-three. The party starts at eight in the evening. Are you coming?
  • Emma: Natürlich! Und Ravi? Er kommt sicher auch. — Of course! And Ravi? He's sure to come too.
  • Jonas: Hast du seine Nummer? — Have you got his number?
  • Emma: Ja: null eins sieben sechs, achtunddreißig, zweiundzwanzig, vierhundertneunundfünfzig. — Yes: 0176 38 22 459.
  • Jonas: Langsam, bitte! Null eins sieben sechs … — Slowly, please! 0176 …
  • Emma: … drei acht, zwo zwo, vier fünf neun. — … 3 8, 2 2, 4 5 9.
  • Jonas: Danke. Oh, wie spät ist es? — Thanks. Oh, what time is it?
  • Emma: Halb zehn. — Half past nine.
  • Jonas: Halb zehn? Mein Seminar beginnt um Viertel vor zehn! Tschüss! — Half past nine? My seminar starts at a quarter to ten! Bye!

Notice:

  1. Dates use ordinal numbers ("fourteenth"), and "on" a date or a day is am: am vierzehnten März, am Samstag.
  2. "At" a time is um: um acht Uhr, um Viertel vor zehn.
  3. halb zehn, literally "half ten", means 9.30: half of the way to ten.
  4. On the phone, zwo is often said instead of zwei, so that it cannot be confused with drei.

docs.title: 3.2 Vocabulary: numbers, days, months and seasons
Numbers from 0 to 20
docs.text:
German German German 0 null 7 sieben 14 vierzehn 1 eins 8 acht 15 fünfzehn 2 zwei 9 neun 16 sechzehn 3 drei 10 zehn 17 siebzehn 4 vier 11 elf 18 achtzehn 5 fünf 12 zwölf 19 neunzehn 6 sechs 13 dreizehn 20 zwanzig

Table 3.1. The numbers from 0 to 20. Switch on Practice and write them from memory.

Look closely at three of them. In sechzehn (16) the s of sechs is dropped; in siebzehn (17) the -en of sieben is dropped. And elf and zwölf are relatives of English eleven and twelve.

docs.text:
German German 10 zehn 60 sechzig 20 zwanzig 70 siebzig 30 dreißig 80 achtzig 40 vierzig 90 neunzig 50 fünfzig 100 hundert

Table 3.2. The tens. Only dreißig is written with ß; sechzig and siebzig shorten their first part, as in 16 and 17.

German 1 000 tausend, eintausend 10 000 zehntausend 100 000 hunderttausend 1 000 000 eine Million 2 000 000 zwei Millionen 1 000 000 000 eine Milliarde (an English billion)

Table 3.3. Big numbers. Careful: German eine Billion is a million million, an English trillion.

docs.text:
German English der Montag Monday der Dienstag Tuesday der Mittwoch Wednesday (mid-week) der Donnerstag Thursday (thunder's day) der Freitag Friday der Samstag Saturday (also der Sonnabend in the north and east) der Sonntag Sunday das Wochenende the weekend die Woche the week der Tag the day

Table 3.4. The days of the week. All of them are masculine, because der Tag is.

docs.text:
German German German der Januar (Austria: Jänner) der Mai der September der Februar der Juni der Oktober der März der Juli der November der April der August der Dezember

Table 3.5. The months. All are masculine. On the phone, Juni and Juli are often said Juno and Julei so that they are not confused.

German English der Frühling spring der Sommer summer der Herbst autumn, fall der Winter winter der Monat the month das Jahr the year

Table 3.6. The seasons, also all masculine.

docs.title: Words for time
docs.text:
German English heute today morgen tomorrow übermorgen the day after tomorrow gestern yesterday der Morgen, morgens the morning, in the morning(s) der Vormittag, vormittags the late morning, before noon der Mittag, mittags midday, at midday der Nachmittag, nachmittags the afternoon, in the afternoon(s) der Abend, abends the evening, in the evening(s) die Nacht, nachts the night, at night die Uhr the clock, watch; o'clock die Stunde the hour die Minute the minute der Geburtstag the birthday

Table 3.7. Words for time.

Common mistake: morgen and der Morgen

morgen with a small m means "tomorrow"; der Morgen with a capital is "the morning". "Tomorrow morning" is morgen früh, never morgen Morgen. And Uhr is the time on the clock, while Stunde is a length of time: Es ist drei Uhr ("It is three o'clock"), but drei Stunden ("three hours").

docs.title: From 21 to 99: the units first
docs.text:
From 21 to 99, German says the units, then und, then the tens, all in one word:

Number Built as German 21 one-and-twenty einundzwanzig 22 two-and-twenty zweiundzwanzig 34 four-and-thirty vierunddreißig 47 seven-and-forty siebenundvierzig 58 eight-and-fifty achtundfünfzig 66 six-and-sixty sechsundsechzig 79 nine-and-seventy neunundsiebzig 85 five-and-eighty fünfundachtzig 93 three-and-ninety dreiundneunzig

Table 3.8. Numbers from 21 to 99.

Note that 21, 31, 41 … begin with ein-, not eins-: einundzwanzig. When you write a number down from dictation, write the second digit first: when you hear vierundsechzig, write the 4 in the units place, then the 6 in front of it. It takes practice; ten minutes a day with prices and phone numbers is the cure.

docs.title: Hundreds and thousands
docs.text: Above 100 the order is the same as in English, and the whole number is still one word: hundertzwanzig (120), zweihundertfünfundvierzig (245), tausendeinhundert (1 100), dreitausendsiebenhundertachtzig (3 780). hundert and tausend have no and: 101 is hunderteins. Only Million and Milliarde are separate nouns with a plural: drei Millionen.

docs.title: Eins and ein
docs.text: When you count, 1 is eins. Before a noun it becomes the article ein or eine ("one" and "a" are the same word in German): ein Kaffee, eine Stunde. In the time, 1 o'clock is ein Uhr or simply eins.

docs.title: Writing numbers: the comma and the point
docs.text:
German uses a comma where English uses a decimal point, and a point or a space to separate thousands:

  • 1,5 is "one point five", read eins Komma fünf;
  • 10.000 or 10 000 is ten thousand.

docs.title: Prices
docs.text:
The euro (der Euro) is the currency of Germany and Austria; one euro is 100 cents (der Cent). Prices are written with a comma and read without it:

  • 2,50 € is read zwei Euro fünfzig;
  • 0,99 € is read neunundneunzig Cent;
  • 12,00 € is read zwölf Euro.

The plural of Euro after a number is Euro: zehn Euro, not zehn Euros. Switzerland and Liechtenstein use the Swiss franc, der Franken (CHF), divided into 100 Rappen: vier Franken zwanzig.

docs.title: Phone numbers
docs.text: Phone numbers are read digit by digit or in pairs, and both are common: 38 22 can be drei acht, zwo zwo or achtunddreißig, zweiundzwanzig. If you are not sure, ask for digits: Einzeln, bitte! ("One by one, please!").

docs.title: Years and ages
docs.text:
Years up to 1999 are read in hundreds: 1989 is neunzehnhundertneunundachtzig ("nineteen hundred nine-and-eighty"). From 2000 they are read in thousands: 2026 is zweitausendsechsundzwanzig. A year stands alone, or with im Jahr, but never with in alone:

  • Ich bin 2004 geboren. or Ich bin im Jahr 2004 geboren. — I was born in 2004.

Age is given with sein ("to be"), as in English:

  • Wie alt bist du? — Ich bin zweiundzwanzig (Jahre alt). — How old are you? I'm twenty-two (years old).

docs.title: Days, months and seasons: am, im
docs.text:
• am + day or part of the day: am Montag, am Wochenende, am Abend, am Morgen (but in der Nacht).
  • im + month or season: im Mai, im Sommer, im Winter.
  • -s for a habit: montags ("on Mondays, every Monday"), abends ("in the evenings"), with a small letter.

am and im are short for an dem and in dem; Lesson 11 explains why.

docs.title: Ordinal numbers and the date
docs.text:
The ordinal numbers (first, second, third …) are made by adding -te to the numbers from 2 to 19 and -ste from 20 upwards. Four are irregular: erste, dritte, siebte, achte.

Ordinal Ordinal 1. der erste 10. der zehnte 2. der zweite 19. der neunzehnte 3. der dritte 20. der zwanzigste 4. der vierte 21. der einundzwanzigste 5. der fünfte 30. der dreißigste 7. der siebte 31. der einunddreißigste 8. der achte 100. der hundertste

Table 3.9. Ordinal numbers. In writing, an ordinal is a number with a point: 3. = dritte.

There are two patterns for the date, and the ending changes:

  • What is the date? Der Wievielte ist heute? or Welches Datum ist heute? — Heute ist der dritte Mai. (written der 3. Mai): ending -e.
  • On what date? Wann hast du Geburtstag? — Am dritten Mai. (written am 3. Mai): ending -en after am.

The day comes before the month, and in figures a date is written day, month, year, with points: 14.3.2026 or 14.03.2026, read vierzehnter dritter zweitausendsechsundzwanzig or, more often, vierzehnter März. A letter is dated Leipzig, 14. März 2026.

docs.title: Telling the time: the official clock
docs.text:
To ask the time, say Wie spät ist es? (how late is it?) or Wie viel Uhr ist es?. The answer begins Es ist …

The official time uses the 24-hour clock: the hour, then Uhr, then the minutes. It is used for timetables, opening hours, the radio and anything formal, and in speech whenever precision matters.

  • 8:00 acht Uhr
  • 9:15 neun Uhr fünfzehn
  • 14:30 vierzehn Uhr dreißig
  • 20:45 zwanzig Uhr fünfundvierzig
  • 0:10 null Uhr zehn

docs.title: Telling the time: the informal clock
docs.text:
In conversation, people use a 12-hour clock with nach ("past"), vor ("to"), Viertel ("quarter") and halb ("half"). The key point is halb: it always looks forward to the next hour. halb drei is "half (of the way) to three", that is 2.30.

Figure 3.1 The informal clock. A clock face. The right half of the dial is labelled "nach (past)" and the left half "vor (to)". At the quarter past position the label reads "Viertel nach", at the half-hour position "halb (+1 hour)", at the quarter to position "Viertel vor". Around the half-hour, two small labels read "fünf vor halb" at 25 minutes past and "fünf nach halb" at 35 minutes past. Below, examples: 2:15 Viertel nach zwei; 2:30 halb drei; 2:45 Viertel vor drei; 2:25 fünf vor halb drei. Time Informal Literally 3:00 drei Uhr or drei three o'clock 3:05 fünf nach drei five past three 3:10 zehn nach drei ten past three 3:15 Viertel nach drei quarter past three 3:20 zwanzig nach drei twenty past three 3:25 fünf vor halb vier five to half-four 3:30 halb vier half-four (half way to four) 3:35 fünf nach halb vier five past half-four 3:40 zwanzig vor vier twenty to four 3:45 Viertel vor vier quarter to four 3:50 zehn vor vier ten to four 3:55 fünf vor vier five to four

Table 3.10. The informal clock. 3:20 and 3:40 can also be said zehn vor halb vier and zehn nach halb vier.

The informal clock does not say a.m. or p.m. Add a part of the day when it is needed: um acht Uhr morgens (8 a.m.), um acht Uhr abends (8 p.m.), um drei Uhr nachmittags. Midday is zwölf Uhr or Mittag; midnight is Mitternacht.

Common mistake: halb

English half three (British, for 3.30) and German halb drei (2.30) are an hour apart. Many travellers have arrived an hour late, or an hour early, because of this. Think of halb drei as "half (of the hour) before three".

docs.title: At what time? Um
docs.text:
To say when something happens, use um:

  • Um wie viel Uhr beginnt der Film? — Um zwanzig Uhr. / Um acht. — What time does the film start? At eight.
  • Der Kurs ist von neun bis zwölf Uhr. — The course is from nine to twelve.
  • Wann kommst du? – Gegen sieben. — When are you coming? – Around seven.

Worked example: an appointment

Ravi has a doctor's appointment on Thursday 12 November at 10.45 a.m. Say it in German in two ways.

  1. Day: am Donnerstag; date: the 12th after am takes -en: am zwölften November.
  2. Time, official: um zehn Uhr fünfundvierzig. Informal: 10.45 is a quarter to eleven: um Viertel vor elf.

All together: Ravi hat am Donnerstag, am zwölften November, um Viertel vor elf einen Termin beim Arzt.

docs.title: Prices and numbers
docs.text:
Read each price or number aloud, then check.

Written Said 1,20 € ein Euro zwanzig 4,75 € vier Euro fünfundsiebzig 0,60 € sechzig Cent 16,99 € sechzehn Euro neunundneunzig 37 siebenunddreißig 71 einundsiebzig 365 dreihundertfünfundsechzig 1990 (a year) neunzehnhundertneunzig

Table 3.11. Practice: read prices and numbers.

docs.title: What time is it?
docs.text:
Clock Informal 7:30 Es ist halb acht. 10:15 Es ist Viertel nach zehn. 12:45 Es ist Viertel vor eins. 6:20 Es ist zwanzig nach sechs. 1:30 Es ist halb zwei. 9:55 Es ist fünf vor zehn.

Table 3.12. Practice: the informal clock.

docs.title: Your week
docs.text:
Read Jonas's week aloud.

  • Am Montag habe ich um neun Uhr ein Seminar. — On Monday I have a seminar at nine.
  • Dienstags spiele ich Fußball. — On Tuesdays I play football.
  • Am Mittwoch arbeite ich von zwei bis sechs. — On Wednesday I work from two to six.
  • Am Samstag, am achtzehnten Oktober, ist meine Party. — On Saturday, the eighteenth of October, is my party.
  • Im Dezember fahre ich nach Wien. — In December I'm going to Vienna.

Say it

Answer aloud: Wann hast du Geburtstag? Wie alt bist du? Wie spät ist es jetzt? Wie ist deine Telefonnummer? ("What is your phone number?"). Give your phone number twice, once in single digits and once in pairs.

docs.title: 3.6 Culture: clocks, calendars and fingers
docs.text:
The 24-hour clock. Timetables, shop signs, invitations and official letters all use the 24-hour clock, and people use it in speech too when they want to be precise: Der Zug fährt um siebzehn Uhr zwölf. In friendly conversation the informal clock is more usual. In parts of eastern and southern Germany and in Austria you will also hear viertel vier for 3.15 ("a quarter of the way to four") and dreiviertel vier for 3.45, following the same logic as halb vier. In Leipzig, where Emma studies, these forms are common.

Dates and weeks. Dates are written day, month, year: 3.10.2026 is the 3rd of October, never the 10th of March. The week starts on Monday, and calendars, diaries and many offices number the weeks of the year: in der Kalenderwoche 42 ("in week 42") is a normal way to arrange a delivery or a meeting.

National days. Each country has its own national day: in Germany, the Day of German Unity (der Tag der Deutschen Einheit) on 3 October, which marks the reunification of 1990; in Austria, the National Day (der Nationalfeiertag) on 26 October; in Switzerland, the Swiss National Day (der Bundesfeiertag) on 1 August, celebrated with bonfires and fireworks.

Birthdays. It is traditionally thought to bring bad luck to congratulate someone before their birthday, so Germans wait until the day itself: Alles Gute zum Geburtstag! ("All the best for your birthday!") or Herzlichen Glückwunsch! ("Congratulations!"). Often the person whose birthday it is brings a cake to work or invites the friends, rather than being treated.

Counting on your fingers. Germans count on their fingers starting with the thumb: the thumb alone is one, thumb and index finger two. If you hold up your index finger to order one beer, you may be understood, but holding up the thumb is clearer. Handwritten numbers differ a little too: the 1 is written with a long upstroke, like an upside-down V, and the 7 has a short line across it so that the two are not confused.

docs.title: 3.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • 0 to 20: null, eins, zwei, drei … sechzehn, siebzehn … zwanzig. Tens: dreißig with ß, sechzig, siebzig shortened.
  • 21 to 99: units + und + tens, one word: fünfundzwanzig (25). 21 = einundzwanzig.
  • Writing: decimal comma (1,5), thousands point or space (10.000). Prices: 2,50 € = zwei Euro fünfzig; plural Euro.
  • Years: neunzehnhundertneunzig, zweitausendsechsundzwanzig; no in: 2004 or im Jahr 2004. Age: Ich bin 22 Jahre alt.
  • When: am Montag, am Wochenende, am Abend; im Mai, im Sommer; um acht Uhr; habits: montags, abends.
  • Dates: ordinal -te (2 to 19), -ste (20+); erste, dritte, siebte, achte. Heute ist der dritte Mai. Am dritten Mai. Day before month: 3.5.
  • Time: Wie spät ist es? Official: vierzehn Uhr dreißig. Informal: Viertel nach, halb, Viertel vor; halb drei = 2.30.

docs.title: Lesson 6: The Present Tense
docs.text:
Das Präsens

The present tense is the workhorse of German. It covers what English says with three different forms, I play, I am playing and I do play, and it is also the normal way to talk about the future: Morgen fahre ich nach Dresden, "Tomorrow I'm going to Dresden". You already know the regular endings from Lesson 2. In this lesson you learn to use them with any regular verb, including those whose stems need a small adjustment, and you meet the verbs that change their vowel in the du and er forms: fahren, du fährst; sprechen, du sprichst; lesen, du liest. You also learn to say what you like doing with the little word gern.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • form the present of any regular verb, including verbs like arbeiten, reisen and wandern;
  • form the present of the verbs that change their stem vowel: a → ä, e → i, e → ie;
  • use the irregular verbs wissen and werden in the present;
  • use the present for the present, the future and actions that began in the past (seit);
  • say what you like and do not like doing with gern, nicht gern, lieber and am liebsten;
  • talk about your free time and hobbies.

docs.title: 6.1 Dialogue: free time
docs.text:
After class, Emma and Ravi have a coffee together.

  • Ravi: Emma, was machst du gern in der Freizeit? — Emma, what do you like doing in your free time?
  • Emma: Ich lese gern, und ich höre viel Musik. Und am Wochenende wandere ich gern. Und du? — I like reading, and I listen to a lot of music. And at the weekend I like hiking. And you?
  • Ravi: Ich koche gern. Und ich spiele Kricket, aber hier spielt niemand Kricket! — I like cooking. And I play cricket, but nobody plays cricket here!
  • Emma: Jonas spielt Fußball. Er trainiert dienstags und donnerstags. — Jonas plays football. He trains on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
  • Ravi: Spielt er gut? — Does he play well?
  • Emma: Ja, sehr gut. Und samstags arbeitet er im Café. — Yes, very well. And on Saturdays he works in a café.
  • Ravi: Wie lange lernst du schon Deutsch? — How long have you been learning German?
  • Emma: Seit sechs Monaten. Und du? — For six months. And you?
  • Ravi: Seit einem Jahr. Aber ich spreche noch nicht gut. — For a year. But I don't speak well yet.
  • Emma: Ach was, du sprichst sehr gut! Liest du auch deutsche Bücher? — Oh, come on, you speak very well! Do you read German books too?
  • Ravi: Ja, langsam. Und ich sehe oft deutsche Filme. — Yes, slowly. And I often watch German films.
  • Emma: Fährst du morgen auch nach Dresden? Jonas und ich fahren um neun. — Are you going to Dresden tomorrow too? Jonas and I are leaving at nine.
  • Ravi: Morgen? Ja, gern! Ich habe Zeit. — Tomorrow? Yes, I'd love to! I'm free.

Notice:

  1. Ich lese gern means "I like reading": the word gern after the verb says that you enjoy it.
  2. Some verbs change their vowel with du and er: ich spreche but du sprichst; ich lese but du liest; wir fahren but du fährst.
  3. Wie lange lernst du schon Deutsch? uses the present, where English uses have been learning.
  4. Fährst du morgen nach Dresden? is about the future, but the verb is in the present.

docs.title: 6.3 Grammar: regular verbs in the present
The pattern
docs.text:
Every regular verb works like kommen in Lesson 2: take the stem (the infinitive without -en) and add the endings.

Person spielen machen lernen Ending ich spiele mache lerne -e du spielst machst lernst -st er, sie, es spielt macht lernt -t wir spielen machen lernen -en ihr spielt macht lernt -t sie, Sie spielen machen lernen -en

Table 6.5. The regular present. Switch on Practice and write the forms.

Figure 6.1 Stem and endings. A diagram of the verb spielen. The stem "spiel" is shown in a grey box, joined to six coloured endings: -e for ich, -st for du, -t for er, sie and es, -en for wir, -t for ihr, -en for sie and Sie. Below, a second row shows fahren with the stem fahr and the forms du fährst and er fährt highlighted: the vowel changes only in these two forms, and the endings stay the same.

docs.title: Three adjustments to the pattern
docs.text:
The endings never change, but three kinds of stem need a small adjustment so that the forms can be pronounced.

1. Stems ending in -t or -d (and a few in -m or -n after another consonant) add an -e- before the endings -st and -t. Without it, er arbeitt could not be heard.

Person arbeiten finden warten ich arbeite finde warte du arbeitest findest wartest er, sie, es arbeitet findet wartet wir arbeiten finden warten ihr arbeitet findet wartet sie, Sie arbeiten finden warten

Table 6.6. Verbs with an extra -e-. Like them: kosten (es kostet), antworten, öffnen (du öffnest), rechnen.

2. Stems ending in an s sound (-s, -ß, -z, -tz) add only -t for du, because the s is already there: du reist, du heißt, du tanzt, du sitzt. So the du form and the er form are the same: du tanzt, er tanzt.

3. Verbs ending in -eln and -ern, such as wandern (to hike) and sammeln (to collect), have the infinitive ending -n, not -en, and so do the wir and sie forms: wir wandern, sie sammeln. In the ich form of -eln verbs the e of the stem is dropped: ich sammle. The rest is regular: ich wandere, du wanderst, er wandert, ihr wandert.

Studieren and the -ieren verbs

Verbs ending in -ieren come mostly from French or Latin, and they are all regular: studieren, telefonieren, fotografieren, trainieren, funktionieren. They are stressed on -ie-: ich studiere [shtoo-DEE-ruh]. Careful: studieren means to study at university, or a subject in depth. For learning a language or for homework, say lernen: Ich lerne Deutsch. Ich studiere Medizin.

docs.title: One present, three English tenses
docs.text:
German has no continuous form (I am playing) and no form with do (I do play, do you play?). One present covers them all:

  • Ich spiele Tennis. — I play tennis. / I am playing tennis.
  • Spielst du Tennis? — Do you play tennis? / Are you playing tennis?
  • Er spielt nicht. — He doesn't play. / He isn't playing.

When you need to stress that something is happening right now, add gerade ("just now"): Ich koche gerade. — I'm cooking at the moment.

docs.title: The present for the future
docs.text:
When it is clear from the context or a time word that you mean the future, German uses the present. This is the normal way to talk about plans and arrangements:

  • Morgen fahre ich nach Dresden. — Tomorrow I'm going to Dresden.
  • Am Samstag arbeite ich. — On Saturday I'll be working.
  • Ich komme gleich! — I'll be right there!

German also has a future tense with werden, which Lesson 15 explains; in conversation the present is far more common.

docs.title: The present with seit: since and for
docs.text:
To say how long something has been going on, German uses the present with seit ("since", "for"), because the action is still going on. English uses the present perfect here:

  • Ich lerne seit sechs Monaten Deutsch. — I have been learning German for six months.
  • Er wohnt seit 2020 in Leipzig. — He has lived in Leipzig since 2020.
  • Wie lange wartest du schon? — How long have you been waiting?

After seit the noun is in the dative case (Lesson 11), which is why you see seit einem Jahr and seit zwei Wochen, seit drei Tagen. Learn these as phrases for now.

Common mistake: Ich habe gelernt seit …

Do not translate I have been learning word for word. Ich habe seit sechs Monaten Deutsch gelernt would mean that you have stopped. If you are still learning, use the present: Ich lerne seit sechs Monaten Deutsch.

docs.title: 6.4 Grammar: verbs that change their vowel, and gern
The stem-changing verbs
docs.text:
A group of very common verbs keeps the regular endings but changes the vowel of the stem in the du and er, sie, es forms. All the other forms are regular. There are three patterns:

Person fahren (a → ä) sprechen (e → i) lesen (e → ie) ich fahre spreche lese du fährst sprichst liest er, sie, es fährt spricht liest wir fahren sprechen lesen ihr fahrt sprecht lest sie, Sie fahren sprechen lesen

Table 6.7. The three patterns of vowel change. The ihr form keeps the vowel of the infinitive: ihr fahrt, ihr sprecht.

  • a → ä: fahren, schlafen, tragen, waschen; and au → äu in laufen (du läufst).
  • e → i: sprechen, essen, helfen, geben, nehmen, treffen, vergessen (to forget).
  • e → ie: lesen, sehen.

A few have extra spelling changes, which you can hear:

  • essen: du isst, er isst (the du form loses its s, as in section 6.3).
  • nehmen: du nimmst, er nimmt (the h becomes mm, because the vowel is now short).
  • treffen: du triffst, er trifft.
  • lesen: du liest (s + st → st).

Dictionaries and the Verb Tables at the end of this book show the er form of every such verb: fahren (fährt), nehmen (nimmt). Not every verb with a or e changes: machen, gehen, kaufen, lernen and stehen are regular. You learn which ones change by meeting them; the common ones are all in Table 6.2.

docs.title: Two more irregular verbs: wissen and werden
docs.text:
Person wissen (to know a fact) werden (to become) ich weiß werde du weißt wirst er, sie, es weiß wird wir wissen werden ihr wisst werdet sie, Sie wissen werden

Table 6.8. wissen and werden.

wissen is "to know" a fact or information: Ich weiß nicht. Weißt du, wo Ravi wohnt? Notice that its ich and er forms are the same and have no ending. To know a person or a place is a different verb, kennen, which is regular: Ich kenne Jonas. Kennst du Wien?

werden means "to become, to get": Es wird kalt. ("It's getting cold.") Jonas wird dreiundzwanzig. ("Jonas is turning twenty-three.") Sie wird Ärztin. ("She is going to be a doctor.") Lesson 15 uses it for the future.

docs.title: Gern: saying what you like doing
docs.text:
To say that you like doing something, put gern (also gerne) after the verb. There is no separate verb "to like" in this construction:

  • Ich koche gern. — I like cooking.
  • Spielst du gern Fußball? — Do you like playing football?
  • Ravi liest gern Krimis. — Ravi likes reading crime novels.

To say you do not like doing something, use nicht gern; to compare, use lieber ("prefer") and am liebsten ("like best of all"):

  • Ich tanze nicht gern. — I don't like dancing.
  • Ich schwimme gern, aber ich wandere lieber. — I like swimming, but I prefer hiking.
  • Am liebsten lese ich. — Best of all I like reading.

On its own, gern also means "with pleasure", "I'd love to": Kommst du mit? – Ja, gern! And Gern geschehen! is "You're welcome!" after thanks.

Worked example: describing someone's week

Describe Jonas's week with er: he studies engineering, trains on Tuesdays, works in a café on Saturdays, reads a lot, likes driving to the mountains, and sleeps a lot on Sundays.

  1. studieren, regular: Er studiert Maschinenbau.
  2. trainieren, regular: Dienstags trainiert er.
  3. arbeiten, stem in -t, extra -e-: Samstags arbeitet er im Café.
  4. lesen, e → ie: Er liest viel.
  5. fahren, a → ä, with gern: Er fährt gern in die Berge.
  6. schlafen, a → ä: Sonntags schläft er viel.

docs.title: Regular or changing?
docs.text:
Infinitive du er, sie, es kochen du kochst er kocht arbeiten du arbeitest sie arbeitet tanzen du tanzt er tanzt schlafen du schläfst sie schläft essen du isst er isst nehmen du nimmst sie nimmt sehen du siehst er sieht wissen du weißt sie weiß gehen du gehst er geht

Table 6.9. Practice: the du and er forms.

docs.title: What do you like doing?
docs.text:
Read the sentences aloud, then say which are true for you, changing the others.

  • Ich höre gern Musik. — I like listening to music.
  • Ich spiele nicht gern Karten. — I don't like playing cards.
  • Ich fahre lieber Fahrrad als Auto. — I prefer cycling to driving.
  • Am Wochenende schlafe ich gern lange. — At the weekend I like to sleep in.
  • Am liebsten treffe ich Freunde. — Best of all I like meeting friends.

Say it

Talk about your free time for half a minute. Say three things you like doing, one thing you do not like doing, what you prefer, and what you like best of all. Add how often: oft, manchmal, nie, jeden Tag. For example:

Ich lese gern, und ich koche oft. Ich tanze nicht gern. Ich schwimme gern, aber ich wandere lieber. Am liebsten fahre ich Fahrrad.

docs.title: 6.6 Culture: clubs, hikes and gardens
docs.text:
The Verein. Much of free time in the German-speaking countries is organised in clubs and associations, the Verein (plural Vereine). There are clubs for football and gymnastics, choirs and brass bands, chess, hiking, dog breeding, local history, volunteer fire brigades and carnival, and a great many people belong to at least one. A sports club is often the centre of village life, with a clubhouse where members meet after training. A popular joke says that when three Germans meet, they found a club.

Hiking. Wandern, walking for pleasure in the countryside and the mountains, is one of the most popular pastimes in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. The countries are crossed by thousands of kilometres of marked footpaths, and the Alps in the south have mountain huts (die Hütte, die Berghütte) where walkers can eat and sleep. Hikers greet each other on the path with a friendly Hallo, or in the Alps with Grüß Gott or Servus.

Allotment gardens. On the edge of many towns, especially in Germany, you will see colonies of small gardens with little huts: the Kleingarten or Schrebergarten. Flat-dwellers rent them to grow vegetables and flowers and to spend summer weekends outdoors. The colonies are run, of course, by a Verein, with its own rules.

Football. Football is by far the most popular sport, both to play and to watch. The German league is the Bundesliga, and Austria and Switzerland have their own national leagues. Winter sports, especially skiing, are a national passion in Austria and Switzerland and very popular in southern Germany.

docs.title: 6.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Regular present: stem + -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en: spiele, spielst, spielt, spielen, spielt, spielen.
  • Adjustments: stems in -t/-d add -e-: du arbeitest, er findet; stems in s/ß/z: du reist, du tanzt; -ern/-eln: wir wandern, ich sammle.
  • Vowel change in du and er only: a → ä (fährt), e → i (spricht, isst, nimmt), e → ie (liest, sieht).
  • wissen: weiß, weißt, weiß, wissen, wisst, wissen. werden: werde, wirst, wird …. kennen = know a person or place.
  • Uses: one present for I play / I am playing / I do play; for the future with a time word; with seit for actions still going on.
  • gern: Ich lese gern. Ich tanze nicht gern. Ich wandere lieber. Am liebsten koche ich.

docs.title: Lesson 16: Review: Putting It All Together
docs.text:
Wiederholung: alles zusammen

You have reached the last lesson of the course. In fifteen lessons you have learnt the sounds of German, its genders and plurals, three cases, the present, the perfect and the future, modal and separable verbs, and the word order that holds it all together, and you have used them to talk about yourself, your family, your town, your food, your day and your travels. This lesson brings everything together. It reviews the verb system and the case system at a glance, collects the mistakes English speakers make most often, warns you about false friends, gives you a first look at the next big step, the subordinate clause, and suggests where to go from here.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • use the twenty most important verbs in the present and the perfect;
  • see the whole verb system of the course in one table;
  • choose the right case after any verb or preposition of the course, with the help of one overview;
  • avoid the ten classic mistakes of English speakers and the common false friends;
  • recognise subordinate clauses with weil, dass and wenn, where the verb goes to the end;
  • write and speak about yourself for a minute or more, combining present, past and future.

masculinefeminineneuterplural

docs.title: The last day of the course
docs.text:
• Frau Wagner: Liebe Kursteilnehmer, heute ist unser letzter Tag. Sie haben in vier Monaten sehr viel gelernt! — Dear course members, today is our last day. You've learnt a great deal in four months!
  • Ravi: Wir danken Ihnen für alles, Frau Wagner. — We thank you for everything, Frau Wagner.
  • Frau Wagner: Gern geschehen. Frau Clarke, was machen Sie jetzt? Fahren Sie nach England zurück? — You're welcome. Ms Clarke, what are you doing now? Are you going back to England?
  • Emma: Ja, nächste Woche fliege ich nach Manchester. Aber im Sommer komme ich wieder, weil ich einen Kurs in Wien machen will. — Yes, next week I'm flying to Manchester. But I'm coming back in the summer, because I want to do a course in Vienna.
  • Frau Wagner: Wunderbar! Und Sie, Herr Kulkarni? — Wonderful! And you, Mr Kulkarni?
  • Ravi: Ich bleibe in Leipzig. Ich habe eine Stelle bei einer Firma gefunden. Im März fange ich an. — I'm staying in Leipzig. I've found a job with a company. I start in March.
  • Frau Wagner: Herzlichen Glückwunsch! — Congratulations!

docs.title: In the flat, that evening
docs.text:
• Jonas: Emma, ich kann es nicht glauben. Du fährst wirklich weg! — Emma, I can't believe it. You're really leaving!
  • Emma: Ja, leider. Aber ich habe hier so viel erlebt. Weißt du noch, mein erster Tag? Ich habe nur „Wie bitte?“ gesagt! — Yes, unfortunately. But I've experienced so much here. Do you remember my first day? All I said was "Sorry?"
  • Jonas: Und jetzt sprichst du fast perfekt Deutsch. — And now you speak almost perfect German.
  • Emma: Na ja, fast. Die Artikel sind immer noch schwer. — Well, almost. The articles are still hard.
  • Sophie, on a video call: Hallo, ihr zwei! Emma, kommst du im Sommer wirklich nach Wien? — Hi, you two! Emma, are you really coming to Vienna in the summer?
  • Emma: Ja, ganz sicher! Ich freue mich schon darauf. — Yes, definitely! I'm already looking forward to it.
  • Sophie: Super, dann kannst du bei mir wohnen. Und Jonas, du kommst auch! — Great, then you can stay with me. And Jonas, you're coming too!
  • Jonas: Natürlich. Also, Prost! Auf Emma! — Of course. So, cheers! To Emma!
  • Alle: Auf Emma! Prost! — To Emma! Cheers!

Notice how much of the course is in these two short scenes:

  1. Tenses: the present for the present and the future (nächste Woche fliege ich), the perfect for the past (Sie haben … gelernt, ich habe … gefunden).
  2. Verb types: modal verbs (ich kann es nicht glauben, du kannst … wohnen), separable verbs (fange … an, fährst … weg, fahren … zurück), a reflexive verb (ich freue mich).
  3. Cases: accusative (einen Kurs, eine Stelle), dative (bei einer Firma, bei mir, Ihnen).
  4. Something new: weil ich einen Kurs in Wien machen will: after weil, the verb goes to the end. Section 16.4 explains.

Twenty verbs to know perfectly
