Table 16.1. Twenty essential verbs. Switch on Practice and test yourself on the forms.

docs.title: Words that hold sentences together
docs.text:
German English Word order und, aber, oder, denn, sondern and, but, or, because, but rather no change (position zero) dann, danach, deshalb, trotzdem then, after that, so / therefore, nevertheless take position 1: verb next weil because verb to the end dass that verb to the end wenn if, when (whenever) verb to the end als when (one time in the past) verb to the end ob whether, if verb to the end

Table 16.2. Linking words and their effect on word order. The last five are explained in section 16.4.

docs.title: Phrases that save a conversation
docs.text:
German English Wie bitte? Sorry? Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? Could you repeat that, please? Können Sie bitte langsamer sprechen? Could you speak more slowly, please? Was heißt … auf Deutsch? What is … in German? Wie sagt man …? How do you say …? Ich habe das nicht verstanden. I didn't understand that. Meinen Sie …? Do you mean …? Ich weiß das Wort nicht. I don't know the word. Einen Moment, bitte. One moment, please. Das ist eine gute Frage. That's a good question. Ich glaube, … / Ich finde, … I think … / In my opinion … Genau! / Stimmt! Exactly! / That's right!

Table 16.3. Phrases that keep a conversation going.

docs.title: 16.3 Grammar review: the verb system at a glance
Five verb forms
docs.text:
The course has taught five ways of using a verb. Here they are with one verb, fahren, and one separable verb, aufstehen:

Form Pattern fahren aufstehen present verb in position 2 Ich fahre nach Wien. Ich stehe früh auf. imperative verb first Fahr langsam! Steh auf! with a modal modal + infinitive at the end Ich muss nach Wien fahren. Ich muss früh aufstehen. perfect haben / sein + participle at the end Ich bin nach Wien gefahren. Ich bin früh aufgestanden. future werden + infinitive at the end Ich werde nach Wien fahren. Ich werde früh aufstehen.

Table 16.4. The verb system of the course. Three of the five forms build a sentence bracket.

docs.title: The present in four families
docs.text:
Person regular: wohnen vowel change: sprechen modal: können irregular: sein ich wohne spreche kann bin du wohnst sprichst kannst bist er, sie, es wohnt spricht kann ist wir wohnen sprechen können sind ihr wohnt sprecht könnt seid sie, Sie wohnen sprechen können sind

Table 16.5. The present in four families.

docs.title: The perfect: two decisions
docs.text:
To form the perfect of any verb, make two decisions:

  1. haben or sein? sein for movement from A to B and change of state (gehen, fahren, kommen, aufstehen, werden), and for sein, bleiben, passieren; haben for everything else.
  2. Which participle? Regular: ge-…-t (gemacht); irregular: ge-…-en (gesehen); separable: -ge- inside (eingekauft); be-, ver-, er- … and -ieren: no ge- (besucht, verstanden, studiert).

docs.title: 16.4 Grammar review: cases, word order, mistakes and false friends
The cases on one page
docs.text:
Case Masculine Feminine Neuter Plural Pronouns nominative der, ein, mein die, eine, meine das, ein, mein die, keine, meine ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie accusative den, einen, meinen die, eine, meine das, ein, mein die, keine, meine mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie dative dem, einem, meinem der, einer, meiner dem, einem, meinem den, keinen, meinen + -n mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen

Table 16.6. The three cases of the course. The bold forms are those that differ from the nominative.

Figure 16.1 Which case? A chart that summarises when each case is used. Nominative: the subject, and after sein and heißen. Accusative: the direct object; after es gibt; after durch, für, gegen, ohne, um; and after the two-way prepositions for movement (wohin?). Dative: the indirect object (the person something is given to); after aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu, gegenüber; after the verbs gefallen, helfen, danken, gehören; and after the two-way prepositions for position (wo?). The two-way prepositions in, an, auf, neben, vor, hinter, über, unter, zwischen are shown in a box between the accusative and the dative.

docs.title: Word order on one page
docs.text:
1. Statement: verb second. Morgen fahre ich nach Wien.
  2. Question with a question word: verb second. Wann fährst du nach Wien?
  3. Yes-no question and imperative: verb first. Fährst du nach Wien? Fahr nach Wien!
  4. The sentence bracket: the second verb (infinitive, participle, separable prefix) goes to the end. Ich muss morgen nach Wien fahren. Ich bin gestern nach Wien gefahren. Ich stehe morgen früh auf.
  5. Inside the bracket: pronouns early; then time – manner – place; nicht near the end. Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug nach Wien.
  6. und, aber, oder, denn, sondern change nothing.

docs.title: A look ahead: weil, dass and wenn
docs.text:
The next big step after this course is the subordinate clause: a part of a sentence that cannot stand alone, introduced by a word such as weil ("because"), dass ("that") or wenn ("if, when"). In a subordinate clause the conjugated verb goes to the very end, and the clause is separated by a comma:

  • Ich komme im Sommer wieder, weil ich einen Kurs in Wien machen will.
  • Ich glaube, dass Ravi recht hat.
  • Wenn das Wetter gut ist, gehen wir wandern.

Compare denn, which you already know, and weil: they mean the same, but only weil moves the verb: … denn ich bin müde, … weil ich müde bin. Notice also the last example: when the subordinate clause comes first, it takes position 1, so the main verb follows straight after the comma: Wenn das Wetter gut ist, gehen wir wandern. For now, recognise these clauses when you hear them; using them freely is the work of level A2.

docs.title: Ten classic mistakes of English speakers
docs.text:
Wrong Right Why (lesson) Morgen ich fahre nach Wien. Morgen fahre ich nach Wien. verb second (7) Ich kann kommen morgen. Ich kann morgen kommen. infinitive at the end (12) Ich habe gegangen. Ich bin gegangen. movement takes sein (14) Ich habe ein Bruder. Ich habe einen Bruder. masculine accusative (8) Der Tisch ist neu. Es ist schön. Der Tisch ist neu. Er ist schön. pronoun follows gender (4) Ich habe nicht ein Auto. Ich habe kein Auto. kein, not nicht ein (5) Ich bin ein Lehrer. Ich bin Lehrer. no article with jobs (5) Ich habe zwanzig Jahre. Ich bin kalt. Ich bin zwanzig. Mir ist kalt. age with sein; feeling cold (5) Ich lerne Deutsch für zwei Jahre. Ich lerne seit zwei Jahren Deutsch. seit + present (6) Ich gehe zu Hause. Ich gehe nach Hause. nach Hause / zu Hause (11)

Table 16.7. Ten classic mistakes. Read the right column aloud until it sounds natural.

docs.title: False friends
docs.text:
German Means Not bekommen to get, receive to become (werden) will want(s) will (werde) also so, therefore also (auch) bald soon bald (glatzköpfig) der Chef the boss a chef (der Koch) das Gift poison a gift (das Geschenk) das Handy mobile phone handy (praktisch) aktuell current, up to date actual (tatsächlich) eventuell possibly, perhaps eventually (schließlich) sympathisch likeable sympathetic (mitfühlend) sensibel sensitive sensible (vernünftig) der Rock the skirt rock (der Felsen) fast almost fast (schnell) das Kind the child kind (nett)

Table 16.8. False friends. Many of them have a related English word with an older or rarer meaning: German bald, for instance, is related to English bold.

docs.title: 16.5 Practice: writing and speaking about yourself
A model text
docs.text:
Read Emma's text aloud. It uses the present, the perfect, modal verbs and the future, and the three cases.

  • Ich heiße Emma Clarke und komme aus Manchester. — My name is Emma Clarke and I come from Manchester.
  • Ich bin Lehrerin, aber dieses Jahr habe ich frei. — I'm a teacher, but this year I'm off work.
  • Seit September lerne ich in Leipzig Deutsch. — Since September I've been learning German in Leipzig.
  • Ich wohne mit Jonas in einer WG. Er studiert Maschinenbau und ist sehr nett. — I live with Jonas in a shared flat. He studies engineering and is very nice.
  • Am Anfang war Deutsch sehr schwer für mich. Ich habe oft „Wie bitte?“ gesagt. — At first German was very hard for me. I often said "Sorry?"
  • Im Dezember sind wir nach Wien gefahren und haben Jonas' Cousine besucht. — In December we went to Vienna and visited Jonas's cousin.
  • Wien hat mir sehr gut gefallen. — I liked Vienna very much.
  • Nächste Woche fliege ich nach England zurück, aber im Sommer komme ich wieder. — Next week I'm flying back to England, but I'll come back in the summer.
  • Ich will dann in Wien einen Kurs machen. Ich freue mich schon! — Then I want to do a course in Vienna. I'm already looking forward to it!

docs.title: Your own text
docs.text:
Write ten sentences about yourself, using Emma's text as a model. Include:

  • your name, where you come from and where you live (present);
  • your job or studies, and your family (present, possessives);
  • your hobbies (gern, lieber, am liebsten);
  • why and how long you have been learning German (seit, denn);
  • two things you did recently (perfect, with haben and sein);
  • something you have to do and something you want to do (modal verbs);
  • a plan for the future (present with a time word, or werden).

Then read your text aloud, record it if you can, and compare it with the text you could have written after Lesson 2.

docs.title: Role-plays
docs.text:
Act out these situations, alone or with a partner. Each brings together several lessons.

  1. At the station (Lessons 3, 11, 15): buy a return ticket to Salzburg for Saturday morning, ask about the platform and whether you have to change.
  2. In a café (Lesson 10): order for two people, ask whether a dish is vegetarian, pay separately with a tip.
  3. Asking the way (Lesson 11): ask a stranger the way to the town hall, and repeat the directions to check.
  4. An invitation (Lessons 12, 13): invite a friend to a party on Friday; your friend can't, explains why, and suggests another day.
  5. After the weekend (Lesson 14): ask a colleague what they did at the weekend, and tell them about yours.

Say it

Talk about yourself for one minute without stopping: who you are, what you do, what you did last weekend, and what you are going to do next summer. Don't worry about mistakes; aim to keep going, and use also, na ja and Moment to gain time, as German speakers do.

docs.title: 16.6 Culture: where to go from here
docs.text:
Keep listening and reading. The fastest way to improve now is to meet a lot of German you can almost understand. Listen to the news in slow, simple German, which several public broadcasters offer; watch films and series with German subtitles; read children's books, graded readers and simple magazines, then move on to the fairy tales of the Brothers Grimm, which are short, famous and written in a clear simple past. Your knowledge of the perfect and of war and hatte will let you follow the story; the other simple past forms soon become familiar.

Speak. Look for a conversation partner: many towns and universities run tandem programmes in which you practise German with a German speaker who wants to practise English. Online, there are many such exchanges. Use what you know, ask Wie sagt man …?, and accept corrections gratefully.

Courses and exams. The Goethe-Institut, Germany's cultural institute, has centres in many countries and offers courses and exams at every level; the Austrian Language Diploma (ÖSD) and the telc exams are other widely recognised certificates. All of them follow the levels of the Common European Framework. After this course you are ready to take an A1 exam and to start working towards A2, where you will learn the subordinate clauses of section 16.4, the adjective endings, the simple past and much more vocabulary.

Go there. Nothing replaces time in a German-speaking country: a language course in Leipzig, Vienna or Zurich, a summer job, a holiday in the Alps or on the Baltic coast. You will hear Saxon, Viennese and Swiss accents, eat Semmeln, Schrippen and Weggli, and discover how far the German of this book can take you. Viel Erfolg und viel Spaß! Good luck, and have fun!

docs.title: 16.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Verbs: present (verb second); imperative (verb first); modal + infinitive at the end; perfect: haben / sein + participle at the end; future: werden + infinitive at the end.
  • Perfect: sein for movement and change; participles gemacht, gesehen, eingekauft, besucht, studiert.
  • Cases: only the masculine changes in the accusative (den, einen); the dative changes everything (dem, der, dem, den + -n).
  • Prepositions: accusative durch, für, gegen, ohne, um; dative aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu, gegenüber; two-way in, an, auf, neben, vor, hinter, über, unter, zwischen (wohin? accusative, wo? dative).
  • Word order: verb second; bracket; time – manner – place; weil, dass, wenn send the verb to the end.
  • Watch out for: the ten classic mistakes and the false friends (bekommen, will, also, Chef, Gift, Handy, eventuell).

docs.title: 16.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Give the perfect, er form, of bleiben.

Answer

er ist geblieben. Er ist geblieben.

Exercise 2

Give the er form of nehmen in the present.

Answer

nimmt. er nimmt.

Exercise 3

Complete: Ich fahre mit ___ Bus zur Arbeit.

Answer

dem. mit dem Bus: mit takes the dative.

Exercise 4

Complete: Das Geschenk ist für ___ Vater. (my)

Answer

meinen. für meinen Vater: für takes the accusative.

Exercise 5

Complete: Wir gehen heute Abend ___ Theater. (into the theatre)

Answer

ins. ins Theater: movement, accusative.

Exercise 6

What does Ich bekomme ein Geschenk mean?

Answer

I get a present. bekommen means to get or receive, not to become.

Exercise 7

Join with weil: Ich lerne Deutsch. Ich will in Wien studieren.

Answer

Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Wien studieren will. After weil, the conjugated verb (will) goes to the very end.

Exercise 8

Put into the perfect: Am Samstag kaufe ich ein, und dann fahre ich zu meiner Oma.

Answer

Am Samstag habe ich eingekauft, und dann bin ich zu meiner Oma gefahren.

Exercise 9

Correct the mistakes: Gestern ich habe gegangen in die Stadt. Ich habe ein neuer Rock gekauft für meine Schwester. Sie ist ein Studentin.

Answer

Gestern bin ich in die Stadt gegangen. Ich habe einen neuen Rock für meine Schwester gekauft. Sie ist Studentin. Verb second after gestern; gehen takes sein; the participle goes to the end; Rock is masculine, so einen neuen (the adjective takes -en here); no article with a job.

Exercise 10

Answer in full sentences: Was hast du letztes Wochenende gemacht, und was machst du nächstes Wochenende?

Answer

A model answer: Letztes Wochenende habe ich Freunde besucht, und wir sind zusammen ins Kino gegangen. Nächstes Wochenende fahre ich mit meiner Familie an den See.

docs.title: 16.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: review of the course

Exercise 11

Gestern ___ ich lange geschlafen.

  1. bin
  2. habe
  3. war
  4. hatte
Answer

habe

schlafen is not a verb of movement or change: perfect with haben.

Exercise 12

Wohin fährst du? – ___

  1. In der Schweiz.
  2. In die Schweiz.
  3. Nach die Schweiz.
  4. Bei der Schweiz.
Answer

In die Schweiz.

A country with an article, movement: in + accusative.

Exercise 13

Ich kann heute nicht kommen, weil ich krank ___.

Answer

bin

After weil, the conjugated verb goes to the end.

Exercise 14

Kannst du ___ helfen? (me)

Answer

mir

helfen takes the dative.

Exercise 15

Match each false friend to its meaning.

ABbekommenbossGiftsoChefto getalsopoison Answer

bekommen — to get; Gift — poison; Chef — boss; also — so

Exercise 16

Put the words in order: "Tomorrow I have to get up early."

Words: früh / Morgen / ich / muss / aufstehen.

Answer

Morgen muss ich früh aufstehen.

Exercise 17

Tap the wrong word.

Ich lerne seit zwei Jahre Deutsch.

Answer

Wrong word: Jahre.

Corrected: Ich lerne seit zwei Jahren Deutsch.

seit takes the dative; the dative plural adds -n: Jahren.

Exercise 18

Translate: I have a brother.

Answer

Ich habe einen Bruder

Exercise 19

Say it aloud.

Nächste Woche fliege ich nach England zurück.

Answer

Say: Nächste Woche fliege ich nach England zurück.

Exercise 20

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Im Sommer komme ich wieder, weil ich einen Kurs machen will.

Answer

Im Sommer komme ich wieder, weil ich einen Kurs machen will.

docs.title: Lesson 1: Sounds, Letters and Spelling
docs.text:
Laute, Buchstaben und Rechtschreibung

German has a reputation for being hard to pronounce, but it is one of the most regular languages in Europe to read aloud. The same letters almost always stand for the same sounds, and the rules fit on a few pages. Most German sounds also exist in English; only three, the vowels written ü and ö and the sound written ch, need real practice. In this lesson you learn the alphabet, the vowels and the umlauts, the consonants that differ from English, the letter ß, the two sounds of ch, where the stress falls in a word, and why German writes every noun with a capital letter. With these rules you can read any word in this book aloud, even before you know what it means.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • say the German alphabet and spell your name and address aloud;
  • pronounce the long and short vowels, the umlauts ä, ö, ü and the combinations ei, ie, eu, au;
  • pronounce the consonants that differ from English, including w, v, z, j, s, sch, sp and st;
  • choose between the two sounds of ch and write ß and ss correctly;
  • place the stress in most German words, and read the sound guides used in this book;
  • use a few classroom phrases such as Wie bitte? and Wie schreibt man das?

docs.title: 1.1 Dialogue: at the language school
docs.text:
Emma has just arrived in Leipzig for a German course. At the office of the language school, Frau Schulz writes down her details.

  • Frau Schulz: Guten Tag! Wie heißen Sie? — Good afternoon! What is your name?
  • Emma: Guten Tag! Ich heiße Emma Clarke. — Good afternoon! My name is Emma Clarke.
  • Frau Schulz: Wie bitte? Wie schreibt man das? — Sorry? How do you spell that?
  • Emma: Clarke: C – L – A – R – K – E. — Clarke: C, L, A, R, K, E.
  • Frau Schulz: Danke. Und Ihre Adresse in Leipzig? — Thank you. And your address in Leipzig?
  • Emma: Goethestraße zwölf. — Goethestraße twelve.
  • Frau Schulz: Goethestraße mit ö und mit ß? — Goethestraße with ö and with ß?
  • Emma: Nein, Goethe mit o und e. Aber Straße mit ß, ja. — No, Goethe with o and e. But Straße with ß, yes.
  • Frau Schulz: Gut. Und Ihre Telefonnummer? — Good. And your phone number?
  • Emma: Langsam, bitte. Noch einmal? — Slowly, please. Once more?
  • Frau Schulz: Ihre Telefonnummer, bitte. — Your phone number, please.
  • Emma: Ah, ich verstehe. Moment, bitte … — Ah, I understand. One moment, please …

Notice:

  1. heißen and Straße are written with ß, a letter that English does not have. It is a sharp s sound, as in English hiss.
  2. The name of the poet Goethe is written with oe, an old spelling of ö: it is said with the ö sound you will learn in section 1.3.
  3. Every noun has a capital letter: Adresse, Straße, Telefonnummer, Moment. So does the polite word for "you", Sie, and the polite "your", Ihre.
  4. Wie bitte? [vee BIT-tuh] is the polite way to say "Sorry? Pardon?" when you have not understood. You will need it often.

docs.title: 1.2 Vocabulary: the alphabet and classroom phrases
The alphabet
docs.text:
German uses the 26 letters of the English alphabet, plus the three umlaut letters ä, ö, ü and the letter ß. The names of the letters are short and regular; many of them are simply the sound of the letter followed by a vowel.

Letter Name Letter Name Letter Name A a ah J j yot S s ess B b bay K k kah T t tay C c tsay L l ell U u oo D d day M m emm V v fow E e ay N n enn W w vay F f eff O o oh X x iks G g gay P p pay Y y ÜP-see-lon H h hah Q q koo Z z tset I i ee R r err ß ess-TSET

Table 1.1. The German alphabet. The umlauts are named by their sound: ä [ai], ö, ü (section 1.3). Switch on Practice to test yourself.

Watch out for the letters whose German names sound like different English letters: German E [ay] sounds like English A; German I [ee] sounds like English E; German A [ah] sounds like English R in British speech; and German J [yot], V [fow], W [vay] and Z [tset] are completely different from their English names. When you spell an e-mail address, the sign @ is at, as in English, or Klammeraffe, and the dot is Punkt.

docs.title: Classroom phrases
docs.text:
German Sounds like English Wie bitte? [vee BIT-tuh] Sorry? Pardon? Noch einmal, bitte. [nokh EYEN-mahl BIT-tuh] Once more, please. Langsam, bitte. [LAHNG-zahm BIT-tuh] Slowly, please. Ich verstehe. [iç fer-SHTAY-uh] I understand. Ich verstehe nicht. [iç fer-SHTAY-uh niçt] I don't understand. Wie schreibt man das? [vee SHRYPT mahn dahs] How do you spell that? (how writes one that?) Buchstabieren Sie, bitte. [bookh-shtah-BEE-ren zee BIT-tuh] Spell it, please. Was bedeutet das? [vahs buh-DOY-tet dahs] What does that mean? Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch? [vee ZAHKT mahn dahs owf DOYCH] How do you say that in German? Ich weiß nicht. [iç VICE niçt] I don't know. Ich habe eine Frage. [iç HAH-buh EYE-nuh FRAH-guh] I have a question. bitte [BIT-tuh] please; also "here you are" and "you're welcome" danke [DAHN-kuh] thank you, thanks ja / nein [yah] / [nine] yes / no

Table 1.2. Phrases for the classroom, and for any conversation in which you are lost.

Bitte, the most useful word

bitte means "please" when you ask for something, "here you are" when you hand something over, and "you're welcome" after danke. A complete polite exchange is just Danke! – Bitte! In shops you also hear Bitte schön and Danke schön, which are a little warmer.

docs.title: How to read the sound guides
docs.text:
The sound guides in square brackets use English spelling. The syllable in capitals carries the stress. A few symbols need explaining:

In the guide Say German example [ah] the a of father, long or short Tag [tahk], danke [DAHN-kuh] [ay] the ay of say, but pure, without gliding into ee Tee [tay] [uh] the weak vowel at the end of sofa bitte [BIT-tuh], Vater [FAH-tuh] [oh] a pure o, as in Scottish go so [zoh] [ü] ee with the lips rounded as for oo für [für] [ö] ay with the lips rounded as for oh schön [shön] [kh] the ch of Scottish loch Buch [bookh] [ç] a soft hiss, like the h of huge said with more breath ich [iç] [eye], [ow], [oy] as in English eye, cow, boy mein [mine], Haus [house], neu [noy]

Table 1.3. The symbols of the sound guides. Everything else is read as in English.

docs.title: Long and short vowels
docs.text:
Every German vowel can be long or short, and the difference changes the meaning of words: Staat (state) has a long a, Stadt (town) a short one. German vowels are also pure: a long German e or o does not glide into another sound as the English vowels of say and go do. Keep your mouth still while you say them.

The spelling tells you the length:

  • Long when the vowel is doubled (Tee, Boot, Haar), when it is followed by an h that is not pronounced (Sohn, fahren, gehen), in ie (Bier, sieben), and usually when it ends a syllable or comes before a single consonant (Name, Tag, gut).
  • Short when it comes before a double consonant (Bett, kommen, Mutter) or before two or more consonants (Hand, Kind, Wurst).
Vowel Long Short a Name, Tag, fahren [ah] Mann, Hand, danke [ah], shorter e Tee, gehen, leben [ay] Bett, essen, Geld [e] as in bed i Bier, ihr, Kino [ee] bitte, Kind, ist [i] as in bit o so, Sohn, Brot [oh] kommen, Sonne, oft [o] as in British hot u gut, Buch, Uhr [oo] Mutter, Hund, und [u] as in put

Table 1.4. Long and short vowels. Listen to each row and repeat.

docs.title: The weak e and the ending -er
docs.text:
An unstressed e at the end of a word or in an ending is weak, like the a of English sofa: bitte [BIT-tuh], Name [NAH-muh], Tasche [TAH-shuh]. Do not leave it out: Tasche (bag) has two syllables.

The ending -er is said as a weak, open [uh], with no r at all: Vater [FAH-tuh], Lehrer [LAY-ruh], Wasser [VAHS-suh], aber [AH-buh]. The same happens to r after a long vowel at the end of a syllable: Bier [bee-uh], Uhr [oo-uh], vier [fee-uh]. A speaker of southern British English already does this in water and beer.

docs.title: The umlauts ä, ö, ü
docs.text:
The two dots over a vowel are called the umlaut (der Umlaut). They change the sound of the vowel, and they make a different letter: schon (already) and schön (beautiful) are different words.

  • ä is like the e of bed when short (Männer, Äpfel), and like the ai of fair, without the r, when long (Käse, spät, Mädchen).
  • ö has no English equivalent. Say a long [ay], as in Tee, and while you hold it, round your lips as if to say oh. The tongue stays where it was; only the lips move. Long: schön, hören, Österreich. Short: können, zwölf, öffnen.
  • ü has no English equivalent either. Say a long [ee], as in Bier, and while you hold it, round your lips tightly as if to whistle or say oo. Long: für, grün, Tür, müde. Short: fünf, Glück, Brücke. The letter y in words such as Typ and Physik has the same sound.
Without umlaut With umlaut Meaning schon schön already / beautiful Mutter Mütter mother / mothers Bruder Brüder brother / brothers Apfel Äpfel apple / apples Ofen Öfen oven / ovens vier für four / for Tier Tür animal / door

Table 1.5. Pairs to hear the umlaut. The last two pairs contrast [ee] with [ü]: keep the tongue still and round the lips.

Writing without umlauts

When umlauts are not available, on a foreign keyboard or in an e-mail address, German writes ae, oe and ue instead: Maedchen, schoen, fuer. That is why the poet is spelt Goethe and why some family names are written Mueller as well as Müller. Never simply leave the dots out: schon and schön are different words. On a phone, hold your finger on a, o or u to get the umlaut letter.

docs.title: Diphthongs: ei, ie, au, eu, äu
docs.text:
A diphthong is a vowel that glides from one sound to another. German has three, and one pair of letters that looks like a diphthong but is not.

Spelling Sound Examples ei, ai [eye], as in eye mein, drei, Wein, heißen, Mai ie a long [ee], as in see Bier, sieben, wie, Wien, Brief au [ow], as in cow Haus, Frau, auch, blau eu, äu [oy], as in boy neu, heute, Deutsch, Häuser, Fräulein

Table 1.6. The diphthongs and ie.

Common mistake: ei and ie

English speakers often mix up ei and ie, and German has many pairs that differ only in this: Wien [veen] is Vienna, Wein [vine] is wine; das Lied is a song, das Leid is sorrow; die Biene is a bee, die Beine are legs. The rule is easy: say the second letter. In ie you hear the name of the letter E in English, ee; in ei you hear the name of the letter I in English, eye.

docs.title: 1.4 Sounds: consonants, ß, ch and stress
Consonants that differ from English
docs.text:
Most consonants are said as in English. These are the ones to learn:

Letter Sound Examples w [v], as in van Wasser, wie, Wien v [f], as in fan, in German words Vater, vier, viel z, tz [ts], as in cats Zeit, zwei, Katze j [y], as in yes ja, Jahr, Junge s before a vowel [z], as in zoo Sie, sieben, Rose s elsewhere, ss, ß [s], as in hiss Haus, essen, Straße sch [sh], as in shop Schule, schön, Tisch sp, st at the start of a word [shp], [sht] Sport, spielen, Straße, verstehen qu [kv] Qualität, bequem pf [pf], both letters heard Apfel, Pferd tsch [ch], as in church Deutsch, tschüss ng [ng], as in singer, never as in finger Finger, lang, Junge h after a vowel silent: it makes the vowel long gehen, John, Uhr

Table 1.7. Consonants that differ from English. The bold letters are the ones to watch.

Four more points complete the picture:

  • sp and st have the sh sound only at the start of a word or of a part of a compound word (Sport, Hauptstraße, verstehen). Inside a word they are as in English: Fenster, ist, Wespe.
  • v in words borrowed from other languages is a [v]: Vase, Klavier, Universität.
  • th is a plain [t]: Theater, Thema. ph is [f]: Physik, Philosophie.
  • r is made at the back of the mouth in standard German, a light gargle in the same place as the [kh] of Buch but softer and voiced (rot, Reise, Frau). Many speakers in the south, in Austria and in Switzerland roll the r with the tip of the tongue, and both are correct. After a vowel at the end of a syllable it becomes [uh], as you saw above.

docs.title: Hard sounds at the end: Tag, Hund, gelb
docs.text: At the end of a word or syllable, b, d and g lose their voice and are said as p, t and k: Tag [tahk], Hund [hunt], gelb [gelp], halb [hahlp], Kind [kint]. When an ending is added, the voice comes back: Tage [TAH-guh], Hunde [HUN-duh], Kinder [KIN-duh]. The same happens to s: Haus ends in [s], Häuser has a [z].

docs.title: The two sounds of ch
docs.text:
German ch has two sounds, and which one you use depends only on the letter before it.

  • After a, o, u and au, ch is the ach sound [kh], made at the back of the mouth, as in Scottish loch: Bach, noch, Buch, auch, acht, Nacht.
  • Everywhere else, after e, i, ä, ö, ü, ei, eu, äu, after a consonant, and in the ending -chen, ch is the ich sound [ç], made at the front of the mouth: ich, nicht, echt, Bücher, Milch, durch, Mädchen, euch.

To find the ich sound, say the English word huge slowly and hold the first sound, with your tongue pressed close to the roof of your mouth; or whisper the y of yes. It is not sh and not k: ich is neither "ish" nor "ick".

Figure 1.1 The two sounds of ch. A chart in two columns. The left column, headed "after a, o, u, au: the ach sound, back of the mouth", lists Bach, noch, Buch, auch and Nacht. The right column, headed "after e, i, ä, ö, ü, ei, eu, consonants, and in -chen: the ich sound, front of the mouth", lists ich, nicht, Bücher, Milch and Mädchen. A note below says that chs is said ks, as in sechs, and that the ending -ig is said like -ich, as in zwanzig.

Two more rules belong here. The group chs is said [ks]: sechs [zeks], wachsen. And the ending -ig at the end of a word is said like -ich in standard German: zwanzig [TSVAHN-tsiç], König, richtig. In southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland you will often hear a [k] instead, zwanzik; both are correct.

The pairs that change the ch

The ch sound can change inside one word family, because the vowel before it changes: das Buch [kh] but die Bücher [ç]; die Nacht [kh] but die Nächte [ç]; die Tochter [kh] but die Töchter [ç]. You do not have to memorise these: follow the rule, and the sound comes out right.

docs.title: The letter ß
docs.text:
The letter ß is called Eszett [ess-TSET] or scharfes S ("sharp s"). It always stands for a voiceless [s], as in hiss. It never begins a word, so it has no ordinary capital form; when a word is written all in capitals, it is usually replaced by SS (STRASSE), although a capital ẞ also exists and is sometimes used.

The rule for choosing between ß and ss is a rule of vowel length:

  • ß after a long vowel or a diphthong: Straße, groß, Fuß, heißen, weiß, draußen.
  • ss after a short vowel: Wasser, essen, Fluss, muss, dass, Kuss.

So the spelling tells you the length: Maße (measures) has a long a, Masse (mass) a short one. In Switzerland and Liechtenstein the letter ß is not used at all: the Swiss write Strasse and gross. If your keyboard has no ß, write ss.

docs.title: Where the stress falls
docs.text:
Most German words are stressed on the first syllable of the stem, the part that carries the meaning: Vater [FAH-tuh], Mutter, Kinder, arbeiten, Bahnhof.

  • Compound words take the main stress on the first part: Bahnhof [BAHN-hohf], Kühlschrank, Telefonnummer.
  • The prefixes be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-, emp- are never stressed: bezahlen [buh-TSAH-len], Geschenk, verstehen [fer-SHTAY-en], erzählen.
  • Words from French, Latin and Greek are often stressed on the last syllable, or on a fixed ending: Musik [moo-ZEEK], Hotel, Student, Büro, Universität [oo-nee-ver-zee-TAYT], Information [in-for-mah-TSYOHN], telefonieren.

German has no written accents, so the stress is not marked; the sound guides of this book show it in capitals.

docs.title: Capital letters
docs.text:
German writes with a capital letter:

  • the first word of a sentence, and names, as in English;
  • every noun: der Tisch, die Liebe, das Essen. This is a great help to the reader: in a long sentence you can see at once which words are nouns;
  • the polite "you", Sie, and its forms Ihnen and Ihr (Lesson 2).

But not the word for "I", ich, unless it begins a sentence, and not adjectives of nationality or languages used as adjectives: ein deutsches Auto, "a German car". Days of the week and months are nouns, so they have capitals, as in English.

Worked example: reading a word you have never seen

Read Schweinebraten (roast pork) aloud, using the rules.

  1. It is a compound: Schwein (pig) + e + Braten (roast). The main stress is on the first part: SHVINE.
  2. sch is [sh]; w is [v]; ei is [eye]: [shvine].
  3. The e in the middle is weak: [uh].
  4. Braten: a long a before a single consonant, [BRAH-ten]; the final -en is weak.

Result: [SHVINE-uh-brah-ten]. Press the button to check: Schweinebraten.

docs.title: Read aloud
docs.text:
Read each group aloud, then listen. Each group practises one rule.

Rule Words Sound w = [v] Wasser, Wein, Woche, wohnen [v] v = [f] Vater, viel, Vogel, vergessen [f] z = [ts] Zug, zehn, Zimmer, Pizza [ts] ei = [eye] eins, zwei, Ei, klein [eye] ie = [ee] Brief, Liebe, spielen, vier [ee] eu, äu = [oy] Euro, Freund, teuer, Häuser [oy] st = [sht] Stadt, Stuhl, Student, stehen [sht] ach sound machen, Kuchen, Woche, Bauch [kh] ich sound Licht, Küche, Kirche, Mädchen [ç]

Table 1.8. Practice: which sound? Switch on Practice and type the sound of each group.

docs.title: Spell it
docs.text:
Spell these names and words aloud in German, letter by letter, then press the button to hear them spelt.

  • Berlin
  • Wien
  • Zürich
  • Jazz
  • Fußball

Say it

Spell your own name, your town and your e-mail address aloud in German. Begin with Ich heiße … ("My name is …"), and finish with Das ist alles. Danke! ("That's all. Thank you!").

Then say these words, which contain all three new sounds: Österreich, München, Bücher, möchten, Küche.

docs.title: 1.6 Culture: one language, three countries and many voices
docs.text:
Where German is spoken. German is the first language of most people in Germany and Austria and of a majority of the Swiss. It is also an official language in Belgium (in a small eastern region), in Luxembourg and in Liechtenstein, and it is spoken by minorities in northern Italy (South Tyrol), in eastern France (Alsace), in Denmark, Poland, Hungary, Romania and elsewhere. Outside Europe there are communities of German speakers in the Americas and in Namibia. Together they make German one of the most widely spoken languages in Europe.

One standard, three national varieties. Germany, Austria and Switzerland each have their own standard form of the language, and all three are correct. They differ a little in pronunciation and in a number of everyday words, as British, American and Australian English do: January is Januar in Germany and Jänner in Austria; a tomato is die Tomate in Germany and often der Paradeiser in Austria; a bicycle is das Fahrrad in Germany and das Velo in Switzerland. The spelling of ß is the clearest written difference: the Swiss write Strasse. This book shows the differences as they come up.

Dialects. Beside the standard language, many regions have their own dialects, which can be very different from it and from each other: a speaker from the far north and one from the Alps may find each other's dialect hard to follow. In German-speaking Switzerland, dialect (Schweizerdeutsch) is the everyday spoken language of almost everyone, and standard German is used mainly for writing, school, the news and talking to foreigners. In Germany and Austria dialects are strongest in the countryside and in the south. You do not need to learn them: everyone learns the standard language at school.

A spelling reform. German spelling was reformed in 1996, with later corrections, by agreement between the German-speaking countries. The best-known change concerns ß: before the reform, ß was also written after short vowels at the end of a word (daß, muß), and you will still see these forms in older books. Today the rule of section 1.4 applies: dass, muss.

docs.title: 1.7 Summary
docs.text:
Summary

  • Alphabet: 26 letters + ä, ö, ü, ß. Watch the names of E [ay], I [ee], J [yot], V [fow], W [vay], Z [tset].
  • Vowels: long when doubled, before h, in ie, or before one consonant; short before two consonants. Pure vowels: no glide.
  • Weak sounds: final -e [uh] (bitte); final -er [uh] (Vater).
  • Umlauts: ä like e in bed; ö = [ay] with round lips; ü = [ee] with round lips. Without the letters, write ae, oe, ue.
  • Diphthongs: ei [eye], ie [ee], au [ow], eu/äu [oy]. Say the second letter.
  • Consonants: w = [v], v = [f], z = [ts], j = [y], s + vowel = [z], sch = [sh], sp/st at the start = [shp]/[sht]. b, d, g at the end = p, t, k.
  • ch: [kh] after a, o, u, au; [ç] everywhere else. chs = [ks]; final -ig = [iç].
  • ß after long vowels and diphthongs, ss after short vowels; Switzerland writes ss everywhere.
  • Stress: first syllable of the stem; never on be-, ge-, er-, ver-; often last in foreign words.
  • Capitals: every noun, and the polite Sie.

docs.title: 1.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Which letter does the German name [vay] stand for?

Answer

W. The German letter W is called [vay], and the letter V is called [fow].

Exercise 2

Is the vowel long or short in Bett?

Answer

Short. It comes before a double consonant, tt.

Exercise 3

Which word means "Vienna": Wein or Wien?

Answer

Wien. Wien [veen]: ie is a long [ee]. Wein [vine] is wine.

Exercise 4

Does the ch of Kuchen (cake) have the ach sound or the ich sound?

Answer

The ach sound. It follows u, so it is [kh]: Kuchen [KOO-khen].

Exercise 5

Does the ch of Küche (kitchen) have the ach sound or the ich sound?

Answer

The ich sound. It follows ü, so it is [ç]: Küche [KÜ-çuh]. Compare Kuchen and Küche: the umlaut changes both the vowel and the ch.

Exercise 6

Fill in ß or ss: Wa__er (water).

Answer

ss. Wasser. The a is short.

Exercise 7

Fill in ß or ss: gro__ (big).

Answer

ß. groß. The o is long. (In Switzerland: gross.)

Exercise 8

How is the d of Hund (dog) pronounced?

Answer

t. At the end of a word, d is voiceless: [hunt]. In the plural Hunde it is a d again.

Exercise 9

Write these words with umlauts: (a) Mueller; (b) Oesterreich; (c) Maedchen; (d) fuenf.

Answer

(a) Müller; (b) Österreich (Austria); (c) Mädchen (girl); (d) fünf (five).

Exercise 10

Mark the stressed syllable: (a) Bahnhof; (b) verstehen; (c) Musik; (d) Lehrer; (e) bezahlen.

Answer

(a) Bahnhof: BAHN-hof (compound: first part); (b) verstehen: ver-STE-hen (ver- is never stressed); (c) Musik: mu-SIK (a borrowed word); (d) Lehrer: LEH-rer (first syllable of the stem); (e) bezahlen: be-ZAH-len.

docs.title: 1.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Quiz: sounds, letters and spelling

Exercise 11

Which letter is pronounced [ts]?

  1. s
  2. z
  3. c
  4. x
Answer

z

z is always [ts], as in Zeit and zwei.

Exercise 12

In which word is ch said with the ach sound [kh]?

  1. ich
  2. Milch
  3. Nacht
  4. Mädchen
Answer

Nacht

In Nacht the ch follows a. In the other words it follows i, l and ä, so it is the ich sound.

Exercise 13

Which word is spelt correctly?

  1. Strasse
  2. Straße
  3. Strase
  4. Strahse
Answer

Straße

The a is long, so Germany and Austria write ß. Strasse is the Swiss spelling.

Exercise 14

Wa___er (water)

Answer

ss

The a is short, so ss.

Exercise 15

Match each spelling to its sound.

ABeioyieoweueyeauee Answer

ei — eye; ie — ee; eu — oy; au — ow

Exercise 16

Tap the word that should not have a capital letter.

Ich Wohne in der Goethestraße.

Answer

Wrong word: Wohne.

Corrected: Ich wohne in der Goethestraße.

Only nouns, names and the first word of a sentence have capitals. wohne is a verb.

Exercise 17

Write Oesterreich (Austria) with its umlaut.

Answer

Österreich

Exercise 18

Say it aloud, with the ü sound.

Für fünf Bücher.

Answer

Say: Für fünf Bücher.

Exercise 19

Write what you hear.

Dictation. Have someone read the sentence aloud, then write it down.

Wie schreibt man das?

Answer

Wie schreibt man das?

docs.title: Lesson 8: The Accusative
docs.text:
Der Akkusativ

In Lesson 5 you met a puzzle: Das ist ein Bruder, but Ich habe einen Bruder. The difference is the case. In the first sentence ein Bruder is in the nominative, the case of the subject; in the second it is the direct object of the verb, the thing or person that is had, bought, seen or wanted, and the direct object is in the accusative case. The good news is that the accusative is easy: only one gender, the masculine, changes its form. In this lesson you learn the accusative of the articles and of the pronouns (me, you, him, her, us, them), the phrase es gibt, "there is, there are", the verb mögen, "to like", and the prepositions that are always followed by the accusative.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • recognise the direct object of a sentence and put it in the accusative;
  • use the accusative of der, ein, kein and the possessives: den, einen, keinen, meinen;
  • use the accusative pronouns mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie, Sie;
  • say what there is with es gibt;
  • say what you like with mögen;
  • use the prepositions für, ohne, durch, gegen, um;
  • describe objects with adjectives and colours, and shop at a flea market.

masculinefeminineneuterplural

docs.title: 8.1 Dialogue: at the flea market
docs.text:
Emma needs a few things for her room. On Saturday morning, Jonas takes her to a flea market.

  • Emma: Ich brauche einen Stuhl und eine Lampe für mein Zimmer. — I need a chair and a lamp for my room.
  • Jonas: Kein Problem. Samstags gibt es hier einen Flohmarkt. Komm! — No problem. On Saturdays there's a flea market here. Come on!
  • Verkäufer: Guten Tag! Suchen Sie etwas? — Hello! Are you looking for something?
  • Emma: Ja, ich suche einen Stuhl. Haben Sie einen? — Yes, I'm looking for a chair. Do you have one?
  • Verkäufer: Ja, hier. Wie finden Sie den Stuhl? Er ist alt, aber sehr bequem. — Yes, here. What do you think of the chair? It's old, but very comfortable.
  • Emma: Hm, den finde ich ein bisschen hässlich. Was kostet der Stuhl da links? — Hmm, I find it a bit ugly. How much is the chair there on the left?
  • Verkäufer: Der? Fünfzehn Euro. — That one? Fifteen euros.
  • Emma: Fünfzehn Euro? Das ist zu teuer. Zehn? — Fifteen euros? That's too expensive. Ten?
  • Verkäufer: Sagen wir zwölf. — Let's say twelve.
  • Emma: Gut, ich nehme ihn. — Fine, I'll take it.
  • Jonas: Emma, schau mal! Hier gibt es eine Lampe für fünf Euro. Ist sie nicht schön? — Emma, look! There's a lamp here for five euros. Isn't it nice?
  • Emma: Doch, sie ist toll! Ich kaufe sie. Und du? Brauchst du nichts? — Yes, it's great! I'll buy it. And you? Don't you need anything?
  • Jonas: Doch, ich suche ein Geschenk für meine Oma. Siehst du den Mann da? Er verkauft alte Bücher. — Yes, I'm looking for a present for my grandma. Do you see the man there? He's selling old books.
  • Emma: Kennst du ihn? — Do you know him?
  • Jonas: Nein, aber meine Oma mag Bücher. Komm, wir fragen ihn! — No, but my grandma likes books. Come on, let's ask him!

Notice:

  1. der Stuhl becomes den Stuhl and einen Stuhl when it is the object: Ich suche einen Stuhl. Wie finden Sie den Stuhl?
  2. The feminine and neuter do not change: eine Lampe, ein Geschenk, mein Zimmer.
  3. "It" for the chair is ihn, the accusative of er: Ich nehme ihn. For the lamp it is sie, which does not change.
  4. es gibt means "there is, there are": Hier gibt es eine Lampe.
  5. After für ("for") the accusative is used: für meine Oma.
